The lab computers run Fedora with Sway, and the examples come from them. At home you may also use Ubuntu: the commands are the same, but some names and defaults differ: Fedora Ubuntu the prompt [student@fedora ~]$ student@ubuntu:~$ the group of the administrators, who may sudo wheel, GID 10 sudo, GID 27 (you are also in adm, cdrom, ...) the . after the permissions in ls -l, context= in id shown: ignore them in this lab not shown the shell of a new user made with useradd /bin/bash /bin/sh, unless you give -s /bin/bash a new home directory drwx------ (700) drwxr-x--- (750) /etc/shadow ----------. root root -rw-r----- root shadow /usr/bin/sudo ---s--x--x. (4111) -rwsr-xr-x (4755) a password not set yet, or locked with passwd -l !! in front of the hash, or alone ! in front of the hash, or alone the umask of a regular user 0022 0002 installing a package sudo dnf install <PACKAGE> sudo apt install <PACKAGE> Ubuntu 25.10 and later use sudo-rs, whose messages differ a little. If your user is not student, use your own name wherever the lab says student.

A user is an account: a name, like student, a home directory, the program that starts when the user logs in, usually a shell, and, if people log in with it, a password. Users keep the work of different people apart: a program that bob starts cannot touch the files of carol, unless she allows it. Services run as users of their own too: a bug in one of them can then touch only its own files. For the kernel, a user is only a number, the UID (User ID); the programs translate it into a name for you.

Command What it prints whoami the name of the user that runs the command id the label of the process: the UID, the primary group (GID) and all the groups id -u, id -g only the UID, only the GID of the primary group id -un only the name of the user, like whoami id -nG only the names of the groups groups the names of your groups, like id -nG id <USER>, groups <USER> what the users and groups databases say about a user: the label they get when they log in [student@fedora ~]$ whoami student [student@fedora ~]$ id uid=1000(student) gid=1000(student) groups=1000(student),10(wheel) context=unconfined_u:unconfined_r:unconfined_t:s0-s0:c0.c1023 [student@fedora ~]$ id root uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root) id printed the label of your shell: the UID, the primary group and all the groups. The members of wheel are the administrators, who may use sudo. Ignore context=...: this lab does not need it. id root printed what the system knows about root, the administrator: the UID 0.
documents.s: Who Am I: whoami and id

documents.t: UID Kind Used for Examples on Fedora 0 root the administrator; the kernel skips most of the checks for it root 1 - 999 system users services; most of them cannot log in, because their shell is nologin bin, daemon, dbus, chrony 1000 - ... regular users people student 65534 nobody files whose real owner is unknown, and processes that must have no rights nobody These ranges are only a convention, set in /etc/login.defs: for the kernel, every UID except 0 is the same.

Every process carries the UID of the user that started it and the GIDs of its groups: the label of the process. Think of a badge: the kernel looks at it every time the process opens a file or sends a signal, and decides if it is allowed. A child inherits the label of its parent: everything you start from your shell runs as you. ps shows the user of every process in the column USER (UID for the number): [student@fedora ~]$ ps -o user,uid,pid,ppid,comm USER UID PID PPID COMMAND student 1000 2817 2805 bash student 1000 3104 2817 ps [student@fedora ~]$ ps -eo user | sort | uniq -c 4 chrony 2 dbus ... 156 root 51 student bash and ps run as student: ps is a child of bash. ps -eo user | sort | uniq -c counted the processes of every user (see Pipes in lab 03): most of them run as root. info ps, ls -l and id get only numbers from the kernel and look up the names; a UID without a user, for example of a deleted user, is printed as a number. note A process can have more than one UID at a time (passwd does). The exercises at home and the challenges need these details: they are in The Credentials of a Process.

A group is a set of users, with a name and a number, the GID (Group ID). A file can give permissions to a group, for example to the students of a project, without opening it to everybody: every member gets them. Every user has: one primary group, which the new files of the user get; useradd creates one with the same name as the user, so student has the primary group student; any number of supplementary groups, for example wheel, the group of the administrators.

The local users are kept in /etc/passwd, one user per line, with the fields separated by :. Everyone can read it: every program that shows a user name needs it. [student@fedora ~]$ ls -l /etc/passwd -rw-r--r--. 1 root root 2245 Oct 20 09:12 /etc/passwd [student@fedora ~]$ head -3 /etc/passwd root:x:0:0:Super User:/root:/bin/bash bin:x:1:1:bin:/bin:/usr/sbin/nologin daemon:x:2:2:daemon:/sbin:/usr/sbin/nologin ls -l showed that only root may change it, but everybody may read it (on Fedora, ignore the . after the permissions). head -3 showed the format. To look up a user, use getent: [student@fedora ~]$ getent passwd student student:x:1000:1000:Student:/home/student:/bin/bash Field In the example What it is 1 student the user name, the one you log in with 2 x the password: x means that it is kept in /etc/shadow (see Passwords) 3 1000 the UID 4 1000 the GID of the primary group 5 Student the GECOS field: the full name, sometimes followed by the room and phone numbers, with , 6 /home/student the home directory: the current directory after login, ~ and $HOME 7 /bin/bash the shell, the program started after login; /usr/sbin/nologin refuses the login

The local groups are kept in /etc/group, one group per line, with 4 fields. Everybody can read it too. [student@fedora ~]$ getent group wheel wheel:x:10:student [student@fedora ~]$ getent group student student:x:1000: Field In the example What it is 1 wheel the name of the group 2 x not used in this lab 3 10 the GID 4 student the members, separated by ,: the users that have it as a supplementary group caution The users whose primary group it is are not listed: the group student has an empty list. Use id <USER> to see all the groups of a user. danger Do not edit /etc/passwd, /etc/group or /etc/shadow with a text editor: one wrong : can stop every user, root too, from logging in. Use the commands from Managing Users and Groups.

Users and groups can also come from a server in the network (LDAP, Active Directory) or from systemd. So the programs do not read the files: they ask the C library (the code that every program uses to talk to the system), which looks in all these places, listed in /etc/nsswitch.conf. Together, these places make the users database and the groups database. getent (get entries) asks the C library in the same way, and prints the result in the format of the files: Command Finds getent passwd <NAME> or <UID> the user with this name, or this UID getent passwd all the users getent group <NAME> or <GID> the group with this name, or this GID getent group all the groups sudo getent shadow <NAME> the line of the user from /etc/shadow, only for root [student@fedora ~]$ getent passwd 0 root:x:0:0:Super User:/root:/bin/bash [student@fedora ~]$ getent passwd nobody nobody:x:65534:65534:Kernel Overflow User:/:/usr/sbin/nologin [student@fedora ~]$ getent passwd alice [student@fedora ~]$ getent passwd 0 found root, and getent passwd nobody found nobody. getent passwd alice printed nothing, without an error: there is no such user. caution Always look up users and groups with getent Use getent passwd and getent group, not cat or grep on the files: the files have only the local accounts. In this lab, the users database means getent passwd, and the groups database means getent group.

root is the administrator, the user with the UID 0. For root, the kernel skips most of its checks: it can read and write any file, signal any process and change the system, so installing software and creating users need it. Its home directory is /root. The kernel looks only at the number: two user names with the UID 0 are both root. This is how an attacker can hide a second root. danger A mistake as root can destroy the whole system: root gets no Permission denied to stop it. Work as a regular user, and become root only for the commands that need it.

sudo runs one command as root. It asks for your password, and it works only for the administrators: the members of one group, whose name depends on the distribution: Distribution The group of the administrators Fedora, Red Hat, CentOS wheel Ubuntu, Debian, Linux Mint sudo To make a user an administrator, add them to this group (see Managing Users and Groups). student is in wheel: [student@fedora ~]$ cat /etc/shadow cat: /etc/shadow: Permission denied [student@fedora ~]$ sudo whoami [sudo] password for student: root [student@fedora ~]$ sudo whoami root cat /etc/shadow failed: only root may read this file. sudo whoami asked for the password of student, then ran whoami as root. The second sudo did not ask again: sudo remembers the password for a few minutes (5 on Fedora), in this terminal. A user who is not an administrator gets bob is not in the sudoers file. sudo logs every command: who ran what, as whom, and from which directory: [student@fedora ~]$ sudo journalctl -t sudo | tail -2 Oct 27 10:02:11 fedora sudo[3311]: student : TTY=pts/0 ; PWD=/home/student ; USER=root ; COMMAND=/usr/bin/whoami Oct 27 10:02:20 fedora sudo[3315]: student : TTY=pts/0 ; PWD=/home/student ; USER=root ; COMMAND=/usr/bin/journalctl -t sudo Command What it does sudo <COMMAND> runs the command as root sudo -u <USER> <COMMAND> runs the command as another user; it asks for your password, not theirs sudo -i starts a login shell of root, in /root, with the variables of root sudo -k forgets that you typed your password: the next sudo asks again sudo !! runs the previous command again, with sudo: bash replaces !! before sudo starts sudo waits for its command to end and passes on the signals it receives. On Fedora, it also runs the command in a new pseudo terminal (see Terminal Emulators in lab 04), so there are two sudo processes. For sudo sleep 300 started from the shell 2817: [student@fedora ~]$ pstree -pu 2817 bash(2817)───sudo(3320,root)───sudo(3321)───sleep(3322) [student@fedora ~]$ ps -o pid,ppid,tty,comm -p 3320,3321,3322 PID PPID TT COMMAND 3320 2817 pts/0 sudo 3321 3320 pts/2 sudo 3322 3321 pts/2 sleep pstree -pu showed the PIDs and, where it changes, the user: everything under sudo runs as root. The second sudo and sleep are on pts/2, not on pts/0: ps -t pts/0 does not find them; use pstree or pgrep. info The new pseudo terminal stops a program started with sudo from typing commands into your terminal after it ends. Before sudo 1.9.14 it was not the default, and pstree shows only one sudo.

su (switch user) starts a shell as another user, and asks for the password of that user: Command What it does su - <USER> starts a login shell of the user: their home directory, variables and groups su - the same, for root; it asks for the password of root exit leaves the shell, back to your own [student@fedora ~]$ su - Password: su: Authentication failure [student@fedora ~]$ sudo -i [root@fedora ~]# whoami root [root@fedora ~]# exit logout [student@fedora ~]$ su - failed: root usually has no password on Fedora and Ubuntu (it is locked, see /etc/shadow). sudo -i started a shell of root with your password; exit left it. With su, everybody who becomes root shares one password; with sudo, everyone uses their own, and every command is logged. Use su to become another regular user. tip The prompt shows # instead of $ in a shell of root. Leave it with exit as soon as you are done.

sudo runs the command, not the whole line. The redirects are done by your shell, which runs as you, before sudo starts: [student@fedora ~]$ sudo echo "192.168.1.20 printer" >> /etc/hosts bash: /etc/hosts: Permission denied [student@fedora ~]$ echo "192.168.1.20 printer" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts 192.168.1.20 printer bash opened /etc/hosts for >> as student, before sudo started, and failed. tee ran as root: it wrote the text from the pipe into the file and on the screen. -a (append) adds at the end, like >>; without it, tee replaces the content, like >. tip To hide the output of tee, add > /dev/null: everybody may write to /dev/null, so this redirect works as you.

/etc/passwd must be readable by everyone, so the passwords cannot stay there. They are kept in /etc/shadow, that only root can read: [student@fedora ~]$ ls -l /etc/shadow ----------. 1 root root 1207 Oct 20 09:12 /etc/shadow [student@fedora ~]$ getent shadow student [student@fedora ~]$ sudo getent shadow student student:$y$j9T$Xr3aB7tPq2LkV9sD1fGh0J$9mQeT4bW1sZxH8cDr5Ny2kLpA7uVq3oEw6iFj0gHt1M:20737:0:99999:7::: On Fedora, /etc/shadow has no permissions: only root, for whom the kernel skips the checks, can read it. On Ubuntu, it is -rw-r----- root shadow. As student, getent shadow printed nothing; with sudo, it printed the line. Each line has 9 fields, separated by :: Field In the example What it is 1 student the user name, the same as in /etc/passwd 2 $y$j9T$Xr3a... the hash of the password; ! or !! in front of the hash means that it is locked; !, !! or * alone means that there is no password: no password works 3 20737 he day of the last password change, counted from 1 January 1970; 0 means that the password must be changed at the next login 4 0 the minimum number of days between two password changes 5 99999 the maximum number of days before the password must be changed, 99999 is never 6 7 how many days before the expiry the user is warned 7 empty how many days after the expiry the account can still be used 8 empty the day when the account expires; empty is never 9 empty reserved chage -l (change age) prints the fields 3 - 8 as dates: [student@fedora ~]$ sudo chage -l student Last password change : Oct 11, 2026 Password expires : never Password inactive : never Account expires : never Minimum number of days between password change : 0 Maximum number of days between password change : 99999 Number of days of warning before password expires : 7 [student@fedora ~]$ date -d '1970-01-01 + 20737 days' Sun Oct 11 12:00:00 AM EEST 2026 note A locked password (field 2) stops only the logins with a password: a user who logs in with ssh and a key still gets in. To stop every login, make the account expire (field 8, chage -E).

The password itself is never stored, only its hash: the result of a one-way function. Computing the hash of a password is easy; finding the password from the hash is not: the only way is to guess a password, hash it and compare. The second field of /etc/shadow has parts separated by $: Part In the example What it is algorithm y the hash function: y is yescrypt, 6 is SHA-512, 1 is the old MD5 parameters j9T the cost of the algorithm: how much work a hash takes salt Xr3aB7tPq2LkV9sD1fGh0J a random text, different for every user, added to the password before hashing hash 9mQeT4bW1sZx... the hash of the salt and the password To check a password, login, sudo or passwd hashes the typed password with the algorithm, the parameters and the salt from /etc/shadow, and compares the result with the stored hash. openssl passwd computes a hash in the same way (-6 is SHA-512): [student@fedora ~]$ openssl passwd -6 -salt Xr3aB7tP pass123 $6$Xr3aB7tP$Z1hKbIRkawX63bJfb3tDz.QpCpVlFdOHOBw1ZdK7Oe/6P0K3E0OUwMhyG7PXhsJPPu.ZobCXoTYNxvAQ3HExk0 [student@fedora ~]$ openssl passwd -6 -salt Xr3aB7tP pass123 $6$Xr3aB7tP$Z1hKbIRkawX63bJfb3tDz.QpCpVlFdOHOBw1ZdK7Oe/6P0K3E0OUwMhyG7PXhsJPPu.ZobCXoTYNxvAQ3HExk0 [student@fedora ~]$ openssl passwd -6 -salt Xr3aB7tP pass124 $6$Xr3aB7tP$msVqpr1xVM/DA2zRy9MVn8yIL5iisMXZpqd3XHD5Ix0aQ5QqD8D3Q91LXVy0w9hPqQLzRYsUVEH5g5oBfNp9// [student@fedora ~]$ openssl passwd -6 -salt Lp0wQ2zM pass123 $6$Lp0wQ2zM$Uo9XUE/86KtNuRc.TcZpxeM0kWUejWZuFOaRQSujvsfACi8WRK55XpaV3Z3WE8TLEWQBF9Jgn4ByzOvO43Ukw0 The same password and salt gave the same hash: this is how the check works. One different letter, or another salt, gave a completely different hash: two users with the same password have different lines in /etc/shadow. info Why is the hash not in /etc/passwd? With a copy of the hash, an attacker can try passwords on their own computer, as fast as it can hash, and nobody sees the tries. A slow algorithm, like yescrypt, and the salt make this harder, but a simple password is still found quickly. So only root can read /etc/shadow, and the programs that check passwords run as root.

Command What it does passwd changes your password; it asks for the old one first sudo passwd <USER> changes the password of another user (only root can do it) sudo passwd -l <USER> locks the password: adds !! (Ubuntu: !) in front of the hash, so no password works sudo passwd -u <USER> unlocks it: removes the !, and the old password works again sudo passwd -S <USER> prints the state of the password: set, locked or empty caution When you type a password in the terminal, nothing appears on the screen. Type it anyway and press Enter. Fedora refuses passwords that are too short or too simple, unless you are root.

These commands change /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow and /etc/group, so they need sudo: Command What it does sudo useradd -m <USER> creates a user, with a group of the same name; -m creates the home directory, -c sets the full name, -s the shell sudo passwd <USER> sets the password of the user sudo groupadd <GROUP> creates a group sudo usermod -aG <GROUP> <USER> adds the user to a supplementary group sudo usermod <OPTIONS> <USER> changes a user that already exists; it takes most of the options of useradd: -c the full name, -s the shell, ... sudo gpasswd -a <USER> <GROUP> also adds the user to the group sudo gpasswd -d <USER> <GROUP> removes the user from the group sudo userdel -r <USER> deletes the user and their group; -r also deletes the home directory sudo groupdel <GROUP> deletes a group; it refuses if the group is the primary group of a user [student@fedora ~]$ sudo useradd -m -c "Dave Brown" dave [student@fedora ~]$ sudo passwd dave New password: Retype new password: passwd: password updated successfully [student@fedora ~]$ sudo usermod -aG students dave [student@fedora ~]$ id dave uid=1003(dave) gid=1004(dave) groups=1004(dave),1003(students) [student@fedora ~]$ ls -ld /home/dave drwx------. 3 dave dave 80 Oct 27 10:15 /home/dave useradd created dave, with the next free UID, a group dave and /home/dave. Until passwd dave, nobody could log in as dave. usermod -aG added him to students, a group made before with groupadd. The numbers may differ on your computer. A new user is not an administrator, so sudo refuses dave, even with his correct password: [student@fedora ~]$ su - dave Password: [dave@fedora ~]$ sudo whoami [sudo] password for dave: dave is not in the sudoers file. [dave@fedora ~]$ exit logout [student@fedora ~]$ sudo usermod -aG wheel dave [student@fedora ~]$ su - dave Password: [dave@fedora ~]$ sudo whoami [sudo] password for dave: root [dave@fedora ~]$ exit logout [student@fedora ~]$ sudo gpasswd -d dave wheel Removing user dave from group wheel The first sudo failed, and the attempt was logged. After usermod -aG wheel, a new login had the new group, and sudo worked with his password. gpasswd -d took the right away. danger Never forget the -a of usermod -aG: usermod -G students dave replaces all the supplementary groups of dave. Run it on yourself and you lose wheel, and with it sudo. usermod changes the fields of a user; userdel -r deletes the user, their group and their home directory: [student@fedora ~]$ sudo usermod -c "David Brown" dave [student@fedora ~]$ getent passwd dave dave:x:1003:1004:David Brown:/home/dave:/bin/bash [student@fedora ~]$ sudo userdel -r dave [student@fedora ~]$ id dave id: 'dave': no such user [student@fedora ~]$ ls -d /home/dave ls: cannot access '/home/dave': No such file or directory userdel refuses a user who still has processes (user dave is currently used by process 4321): log the user out first.

When you log in, a process gets the UID and the groups of your user. On a text terminal, like /dev/tty3: systemd starts agetty on the terminal, as root; it prints login: and reads the user name; agetty becomes login (it runs exec), still as root, and it asks for the password; login finds the user in the users database, and checks the password with the hash from /etc/shadow; a child of login sets its groups and, at the end, its UID to the ones of the user; after that, it can never go back to root; the child changes to the home directory and runs (exec) the shell from /etc/passwd. [student@fedora ~]$ ps -t tty3 -o user,pid,ppid,comm USER PID PPID COMMAND root 5120 1 login student 5191 5120 bash login stays as root and waits for the shell, which runs as student. A graphical login, ssh and su do the same steps. info A new group needs a new login The groups enter the label of a process only at login, and with su and sudo. After you are added to a group, the programs that already run, and the terminals they open, do not have it: log out and log in again, or start a login shell with su - student. id student reads the database and shows the new group at once; id shows the label of your shell.

Every file has one owner (a user), one group, and three sets of permissions: for the owner (u, user), the group (g) and the others (o). The owner does not have to be in the group. ls -l shows them: [student@fedora lab05]$ ls -l notes.txt -rw-r-----. 1 student students 9 Oct 27 10:20 notes.txt Part In the example What it is type - - a file, d a directory, l a symbolic link, c and b devices u rw- the owner, student, can read and write the file g r-- the members of the group students can only read it o --- everybody else can do nothing owner student the user that owns the file, usually the one that created it group students the group of the file, usually the primary group of the one that created it stat prints them in the format you ask for: [student@fedora lab05]$ stat -c '%A %a %U %G %n' notes.txt /etc/passwd /etc/shadow -rw-r----- 640 student students notes.txt -rw-r--r-- 644 root root /etc/passwd ---------- 0 root root /etc/shadow %A are the permissions as letters, %a as a number (see chmod), %U the owner, %G the group and %n the name.

The same letters have a different meaning for files and for directories: Permission Value For a file For a directory r read 4 read the content (cat, less) list the names of the files inside (ls) w write 2 change the content create, delete and rename the files inside; it works only together with x x execute 1 run it as a program enter it (cd) and reach the files inside, if you know their names A directory is a list of names: r reads the list, w changes it, and x uses it to reach a file. So: deleting or renaming a file changes the directory, not the file: with w on a directory you can delete a file that you cannot even read; to reach a file you need x on every directory of its path: cat /home/student/lab05/notes.txt needs x on /, /home, /home/student and /home/student/lab05; ls -l needs x too: it reaches every file to read its details. [student@fedora lab05]$ ls -ld noread noenter d--x------. 2 student student 60 Oct 27 10:20 noread dr--------. 2 student student 60 Oct 27 10:20 noenter [student@fedora lab05]$ ls noread ls: cannot open directory 'noread': Permission denied [student@fedora lab05]$ cat noread/secret.txt top secret [student@fedora lab05]$ ls noenter ls: cannot access 'noenter/secret.txt': Permission denied secret.txt [student@fedora lab05]$ cd noenter bash: cd: noenter: Permission denied noread (x, no r): ls failed, but cat opened a file whose name it knew. noenter (r, no x): ls read the name, but could not reach the file to color it, so it also printed an error; cd failed. info Home directories are drwx------ on Fedora: the other users cannot reach your files at all. On Ubuntu they are drwxr-x--- (an older Ubuntu may have drwxr-xr-x): check yours with ls -ld ~.

The kernel checks these rules in order, and the first match decides: if the user of the process is root, the UID 0: everything is allowed (except running a file without any x); if the user of the process is the owner of the file: the u permissions are used; if one of the groups of the process is the group of the file: the g permissions are used; otherwise: the o permissions are used. For notes.txt above, -rw-r----- student students: Process run by Its groups Uses Read Write root root - yes yes student student, wheel u yes yes bob bob, students g yes no carol carol o no no caution Only one set is used: with ----rw----, the owner can do nothing, even if they are in the group.

chmod (change mode) changes the permissions; only the owner (or root) may run it. With letters: Part Letters who u the owner, g the group, o the others (not the owner and not in the group), a all three how + adds, - removes, = sets exactly these what r, w, x Command What it does chmod u+x script.sh adds x for the owner chmod +x script.sh adds x for everybody, except where the umask blocks it chmod g+w,o-r notes.txt adds w for the group and removes r for the others chmod go-rwx notes.txt removes everything for the group and the others chmod a=r readme.txt sets r-- for everybody chmod u=rw,go=r notes.txt sets exactly rw-r--r--: = replaces the old permissions instead of adding to them chmod -R g+rX project for project and everything inside: adds r for the group, and x only to the directories and to the files that already have an x for someone With numbers, in octal: r is 4, w is 2, x is 1, added for each of u, g and o: Letters u g o Number rw-r----- 4 + 2 = 6 4 = 4 0 640 rwxr-xr-x 4 + 2 + 1 = 7 4 + 1 = 5 4 + 1 = 5 755 rw-r--r-- 6 4 4 644 rw------- 6 0 0 600 [student@fedora lab05]$ ls -l myid.sh -rw-r--r--. 1 student student 18 Oct 27 10:20 myid.sh [student@fedora lab05]$ ./myid.sh bash: ./myid.sh: Permission denied [student@fedora lab05]$ chmod u+x myid.sh [student@fedora lab05]$ ./myid.sh student [student@fedora lab05]$ chmod 600 myid.sh [student@fedora lab05]$ ls -l myid.sh -rw-------. 1 student student 18 Oct 27 10:20 myid.sh ./myid.sh failed without x; after chmod u+x, it ran. chmod 600 set all the permissions at once. tip Use letters to change some permissions (chmod g+w), and numbers to set all of them (chmod 640). With -R, use letters: chmod -R 644 box also removes the x of the directories, so nobody can enter them; chmod -R u=rwX,go=rX box gives rw-r--r-- to the files and rwxr-xr-x to the directories.

A program asks for rw-rw-rw- (666) for a new file and rwxrwxrwx (777) for a new directory; the kernel then removes the bits of the umask of the process. umask is a built-in command of the shell (help umask), inherited by every child. [student@fedora lab05]$ umask 0022 [student@fedora lab05]$ touch new.txt [student@fedora lab05]$ mkdir newdir [student@fedora lab05]$ ls -ld new.txt newdir -rw-r--r--. 1 student student 0 Oct 27 10:25 new.txt drwxr-xr-x. 2 student student 40 Oct 27 10:25 newdir File Directory the program asks for 666 rw-rw-rw- 777 rwxrwxrwx umask 022 removes 022 ----w--w- 022 ----w--w- the result 644 rw-r--r-- 755 rwxr-xr-x A new file is never executable: umask only removes bits. umask 077 makes new files 600 and new directories 700, until the shell ends.

Command What it does sudo chown bob notes.txt the owner becomes bob sudo chown bob:students notes.txt the owner becomes bob and the group students chown :students notes.txt only the group, like chgrp chgrp students notes.txt only the group chown -R, chgrp -R the directory and everything inside it sudo chown 1005 notes.txt the owner becomes the UID 1005, even if there is no user with it Only root can give a file to another user. The owner can change the group of a file only to one of the groups of their process. [student@fedora lab05]$ chown carol notes.txt chown: changing ownership of 'notes.txt': Operation not permitted [student@fedora lab05]$ sudo chown carol notes.txt [student@fedora lab05]$ ls -l notes.txt -rw-r-----. 1 carol students 9 Oct 27 10:20 notes.txt

There are three more bits, shown by ls -l in the place of an x: Bit Number ls -l shows On a program On a directory setuid 4000 -rwsr-xr-x runs as the owner of the file ignored setgid 2000 -rwxr-sr-x, drwxrwsr-x runs with the group of the file new files get the group of the directory; new directories also get the bit sticky 1000 drwxrwxrwt ignored a file can be deleted or renamed only by its owner, the owner of the directory and root With letters, they are u+s, g+s and +t; with numbers, the 4th digit in front: chmod 2775 project is rwxrwsr-x. A capital S or T means that the bit is set, but the x under it is not.

passwd must write /etc/shadow, which only root can change. /usr/bin/passwd belongs to root and has the setuid bit: whoever starts it, it runs as root. [student@fedora ~]$ ls -l /usr/bin/passwd /usr/bin/sudo /usr/bin/su -rwsr-xr-x. 1 root root 32648 Jul 24 03:00 /usr/bin/passwd -rwsr-xr-x. 1 root root 56920 Jul 24 03:00 /usr/bin/su ---s--x--x. 1 root root 262536 Jul 24 03:00 /usr/bin/sudo sudo and su are setuid programs too. Run passwd in one terminal, without typing anything, and look at it from another one: [student@fedora ~]$ ps -o pid,ruser,user,comm -C passwd PID RUSER USER COMMAND 6011 student root passwd passwd runs as root (USER), so it may write /etc/shadow; the kernel also keeps who started it (RUSER, the real user), so passwd changes only your password. See The Credentials of a Process. danger Never add +s to a program of root: it then runs as root for everybody, and one bug in it makes anybody root. info The kernel ignores the setuid and setgid bits on scripts: it starts /bin/bash, which then opens the script by its name, and in between a user could replace the file.

In a shared directory, the new files should get the group of the project, not the primary group of each user. The setgid bit on the directory does this: [student@fedora ~]$ sudo mkdir /srv/project [student@fedora ~]$ sudo chgrp students /srv/project [student@fedora ~]$ sudo chmod 2775 /srv/project [student@fedora ~]$ ls -ld /srv/project drwxrwsr-x. 2 root students 40 Oct 27 10:40 /srv/project [student@fedora ~]$ sudo -u bob touch /srv/project/bob.txt [student@fedora ~]$ ls -l /srv/project total 0 -rw-r--r--. 1 bob students 0 Oct 27 10:41 bob.txt bob.txt got the group of the directory, students, not bob. caution If you are not in the group of the directory, set the bit as root: otherwise the kernel silently removes it.

Everyone has w on /tmp, so anyone could delete the files of the others. The sticky bit, t, allows only the owner of the file, the owner of the directory and root to delete or rename a file: [student@fedora ~]$ ls -ld /tmp drwxrwxrwt. 21 root root 520 Oct 27 10:00 /tmp tip find can look for the special bits: find /usr -perm -4000 prints the files that have at least the setuid bit.

The prompt of bash is built from the shell variable PS1 (see Shell Variables in lab 04). On Fedora, it is [\u@\h \W]\$ ; on Ubuntu, it is longer, but without the colors it comes down to \u@\h:\w\$ : Escape Meaning For student For root \u the user student root \h the host name fedora fedora \W the name of the current directory (\w is the whole path) lab05 ~ \$ $ for the users, # for the UID 0 $ # The prompt is only text, and any user can change it: [student@fedora ~]$ PS1='[root@fedora \W]# ' [root@fedora ~]# whoami student [root@fedora ~]# cat /etc/shadow cat: /etc/shadow: Permission denied caution Do not trust the prompt to tell you who you are. whoami and id ask the kernel for the label of the process.

PS1 can hold any text, and these escapes (man bash, section PROMPTING): Escape Replaced with \u, \h the user; the host name, up to the first . \w, \W the whole path of the current directory, with ~ for your home; only its last name \$ $, or # if the UID is 0 \t, \A the time, as HH:MM:SS and HH:MM \d the date, like Tue Oct 27 \j the number of jobs of the shell (lab 04) \n a new line [student@fedora lab05]$ PS1='\A \u in \w \$ ' 10:52 student in ~/lab05 $ PS1='[\u@\h \W]\$ ' [student@fedora lab05]$ tip A change of PS1 lasts until the shell ends; to keep it, add PS1='...' at the end of ~/.bashrc.

note Going deeper You do not need this section for the exercises of the lab, the 🧪 First Steps. Read it at home: the 🏠 Going Further exercises and the 📝 Challenges use it. For every process, the kernel keeps its credentials: four UIDs, four GIDs and the supplementary groups. Only the kernel changes them, by strict rules. Credential What it is real UID and GID the user who started the process, and their primary group; programs read them to find out who you are effective UID and GID the ones that the kernel checks, when the process opens a file; ps shows the effective user in the column USER saved UID and GID a spare copy of the effective ones, made when the program starts, so that it can put its rights aside for a while and take them back file system UID and GID used only for files; on Linux, they always follow the effective ones, so you can ignore them supplementary groups the other groups of the process, checked together with the effective GID; copied from the groups database at login, and by su and sudo For your shell, all the UIDs and GIDs are 1000. They differ in two cases: a setuid program changes the effective and the saved UID, but not the real one; login, su and sudo change all of them for the program they start.

What the kernel checks depends on what the process asks for: opening a file: the effective UID is compared with the owner of the file, and the effective GID and the supplementary groups with the group of the file (see Which Permissions Apply?); sending a signal, with kill: the real or the effective UID of the sender must be the real or the saved UID of the target. You can end a passwd that you started, even if it runs as root, because its real UID is yours; bob cannot; changing its own UIDs: a process that is not root may only take a UID that it already has, its real, its effective or its saved one. A process cannot make itself root. Only a process whose effective UID is 0 may take any UID.

What happens to the UIDs at each step of the life of a process: When What happens to the UIDs fork, a new child the child gets a copy of the credentials of its parent exec of a regular program nothing changes exec of a program with the setuid bit the effective and the saved UID become the owner of the file; the real UID does not change; the setgid bit does the same for the GIDs, with the group of the file a process whose effective UID is 0 calls setgid(), initgroups() and setuid() all the GIDs, the supplementary groups and all the UIDs change, in this order: this is how login, su and sudo give a process the label of a user (see Logging In and sudo)

There are two ways to see the credentials of a process: [student@fedora ~]$ ps -o pid,ruser,euser,suser,comm -p $$ PID RUSER EUSER SUSER COMMAND 2817 student student student bash [student@fedora ~]$ grep -E '^(Uid|Gid|Groups):' /proc/$$/status Uid: 1000 1000 1000 1000 Gid: 1000 1000 1000 1000 Groups: 10 1000 ps -o took the names of the columns: ruser is the real user, euser the effective one and suser the saved one. man ps lists all of them, for the UIDs, the GIDs and the groups, in the section STANDARD FORMAT SPECIFIERS. The Uid: and Gid: lines of /proc/<PID>/status have 4 numbers: real, effective, saved and file system; Groups: has the supplementary groups (man 5 proc). Everybody can read the status file of any process. A process cannot make itself root. python3 can read its UIDs with os.getresuid() and try to change them with os.setuid(): [student@fedora ~]$ python3 -c 'import os; print(os.getresuid()); os.setuid(0)' (1000, 1000, 1000) Traceback (most recent call last): File "<string>", line 1, in <module> import os; print(os.getresuid()); os.setuid(0) ~~~~~~~~~^^^ PermissionError: [Errno 1] Operation not permitted The kernel refused: 0 is none of the UIDs of the process. To get root, a process must start a setuid program of root (sudo, su, passwd) or be started by a process that already runs as root (login).

A careful setuid program works as you, and uses root only for the steps that need it, so that a bug elsewhere can do only what you could do. The saved UID makes this possible. After the exec, its Uid: line is 1000 0 0 0: the program sets its effective UID to its real one, 1000 (Uid: 1000 1000 0 1000): root stays only in the saved UID; when it needs root again, it sets its effective UID back to 0 (Uid: 1000 0 0 0): this is allowed, because 0 is its saved UID; when it does not need root any more, it sets all three UIDs to 1000 (Uid: 1000 1000 1000 1000): 0 is none of its UIDs now, so it can never go back.

With the right permissions, bob runs it and it prints bob; carol can neither read it nor run it. → r, w and x Known names only: Hide a file in a directory, so that only those who know its name can read it. /srv/lab05/hidden, with the file key.txt: the members of students can read key.txt if they know its name, but cannot list the directory; nobody else can do anything. Check: bob can print hidden/key.txt, but ls hidden is denied; carol cannot reach key.txt, even with its name. → r, w and x A private list: Help bob share a file from his home directory with his group, and with nobody else. As bob: close /home/bob to everybody except bob (it is already like this on Fedora, not on Ubuntu); create /home/bob/todo.txt with the text Bob's TODO list, readable and writable only by bob; check that carol cannot read it; change it so that the members of the group bob can also read it, and nobody else can do anything; leave, add yourself (student) to the group bob, and try to read the file from a new login shell; find out why it still fails, and let bob change the right directory so that it works, without letting carol in; remove yourself from the group bob. Check: at step 3 it is still denied, although you are in the group bob and the file gives its group r: look at every directory of the path. After the fix you can read the file, but you cannot list /home/bob, and carol still gets nothing. → Which Permissions Apply? · r, w and x The prompt A prompt that tells the truth, and stays: Unlike the fake root of the First Steps, make a prompt that shows the UID of the shell, so that it changes by itself, and keep it for every new terminal. make a prompt that shows your UID, from a variable of bash, and the $ or #; start a login shell of root, set the same PS1 in it, and look at the prompt; leave it; add your PS1 at the end of ~/.bashrc, open a new terminal, and check the prompt; start a login shell of root, and look at its prompt. 💡 man bash: search for EUID; write PS1 between single quotes, so that the variable is replaced every time the prompt is shown, not once when you set it. Check: your prompt shows 1000 and $; the shell of root shows 0 and #: \$ and $EUID come from the label of the shell, not from a text you typed. The new terminal has your prompt; the shell of root does not: it reads /root/.bashrc, not yours. → Changing the Prompt Clean up Clean up: Leave the system as it was before the lab. delete the users bob and carol, with their home directories, and the group students; delete /srv/lab05 and /tmp/student.txt; delete ~/lab05 (if it fails, find out which directory has no w or x for you); remove your PS1 from ~/.bashrc. Check: id bob, id carol and getent group students find nothing; /srv does not have lab05. → Managing Users and Groups

These exercises are like the ones at the exam. Each one gives you a result to reach and the rules you must follow, but not the steps: you decide the commands. Each one ends with the Check that will be used to grade it. Many of them need The Credentials of a Process. All the challenges start from the same setup, the one you will find at the exam: the users bob, carol and dave, the group students, with bob and dave as members, and the empty directory /srv/exam, owned by root. Copy and run these commands once, before the first challenge (they do not change the users and the groups that exist already): sudo groupadd -f students for u in bob carol dave; do id "$u" &> /dev/null || sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash "$u"; done sudo usermod -aG students bob sudo usermod -aG students dave sudo mkdir -p /srv/exam The users have no passwords: run commands as them with sudo -u <USER>. When you are done with all the challenges, remove everything with: sudo rm -rf /srv/exam for u in bob carol dave grace; do id "$u" &> /dev/null && sudo userdel -r "$u"; done sudo groupdel students An offline attack: See how a hash depends on the password and on the salt, then find a password from its hash, the way an attacker with a copy of /etc/shadow would. hash the password pass123 with SHA-512 and the salt abc, twice; then with the salt xyz; then hash pass124 with the salt abc; a user has this line in a stolen copy of /etc/shadow: mallory:$6$uso2026$YT5ail.RilPFhAJ4Zo6bXZ6qayzFgl959rpxQZDutFYsI3F/Yq4zt5BFc04bFuFJN7PE9Scof6J8VZUPjp7Y20:20737:0:99999:7::: you know that the password is one of 123456, password, qwerty, dragon and letmein; find which one, with one command line; explain why /etc/shadow must not be readable by everybody. 💡 man openssl-passwd: search for SHA512 and for salt; one command can hash several passwords. Find the algorithm and the salt in the hash of mallory; man grep: search for line-number. Check: in step 1, the first two hashes are the same; another salt, or one different letter, gives a completely different hash. In step 2, your command line prints exactly one hash, the one of mallory, with its line number; the line number tells you the password. Anybody who can read a hash can try passwords on it, offline and unseen: this is why only root may read /etc/shadow. → Hashes and Salt Predict the credentials: Predict all the UIDs and GIDs of three processes, check them with a single command, and find every process that has the power of root and was started from a terminal. The three processes: your shell, a sleep 300 started as bob with sudo, and a passwd waiting for a password. first fill in the table below on paper, from How the Credentials Change; start the two processes in other terminals; print, in one ps command, a column for each of: the real, effective, saved and file system UID, and the real and effective GID, for the three processes; compare; find all the processes that run with the effective user root but have a terminal, and show for each its terminal, its real and effective user, and its command. 💡 man ps, STANDARD FORMAT SPECIFIERS: search for saved and for filesystem; -p takes several PIDs, separated by ,; the processes without a terminal have ? in the TTY column. Check: the shell has 1000 everywhere; sleep has the UID of bob everywhere, and the GID of bob; passwd has the real UID 1000 and the other three 0, and the GIDs 1000: it has only the setuid bit, not the setgid one. In step 3 you see the agetty of the virtual terminals that you opened, but where nobody is logged in, the login of every one where somebody is, the sudo, su and passwd that are still running, and the shells of root; the real user tells you who started each of them. → The Credentials of a Process Who can do what: Predict which users may open which files, and who may end which process, then prove each answer with one command. Create two files with these commands: printf 'file a\n' | sudo tee /srv/exam/a.txt > /dev/null printf 'file b\n' | sudo tee /srv/exam/b.txt > /dev/null sudo chown root:students /srv/exam/a.txt sudo chmod 640 /srv/exam/a.txt sudo chown bob:students /srv/exam/b.txt sudo chmod 064 /srv/exam/b.txt Then start these processes; run passwd in a second terminal, and do not type anything: sudo -b -u bob sleep 601 sudo -b sleep 602 first, on paper: for student, bob, carol and dave, can they read a.txt? Read b.txt? Write b.txt? first, on paper: for student, bob and carol, can they end sleep 601? sleep 602? passwd? prove every answer of the two tables with one command each, as the right user; end the three processes. 💡 man sudo: search for background; man pgrep: search for full, to find a process by its whole command line; man 2 kill: search for If sig is 0, to test if you may send a signal without sending one. Check: the files: read a.txt read b.txt write b.txt student no yes no bob yes no no carol no yes no dave yes yes yes bob owns b.txt, so he gets the u set, ---, even if his group may write it. The processes: student may end only passwd, whose real UID is his; bob may end only sleep 601, which runs with all his UIDs; carol may end none; nobody but root may end sleep 602. Each answer must come from a command that prints the content or an error (Permission denied, Operation not permitted). → Which Permissions Apply? · Which Credentials Are Checked A project for the group: Build a project directory for a group, where the files belong to the group and nobody can delete the work of the others. Make /srv/exam/project so that: root owns it, and only the members of students can enter it, list it and create files in it; every new file in it belongs to the group students, whoever creates it; a member cannot delete or rename the files of another member. Check: stat -c '%A %U %G' /srv/exam/project prints drwxrws--T root students: you needed two special bits. A file created by bob and one created by dave both have the group students, although their primary groups are bob and dave; bob gets Operation not permitted when he deletes the file of dave; carol gets Permission denied when she lists the directory. → setgid on a Directory · The Sticky Bit A homework box: Build a box where the students hand in their homework, without seeing the names of the files of the others or changing them, while the teacher may still clean it. Make /srv/exam/homework so that: student, the teacher, owns it and can do everything in it; the members of students can hand in files (create them), but cannot list the directory, so they cannot see the names of the others; they cannot delete or replace the files of the others, even if they guess the names; carol can do nothing. Hand in bob.txt as bob, and dave.txt as dave; as bob, try to list the directory, to delete dave.txt, and to print it; then, as the teacher, delete dave.txt. Check: stat -c '%A %U %G' /srv/exam/homework prints drwx-wx--T student students. bob can create files, but cannot list the directory or delete dave.txt (Operation not permitted); he can print dave.txt, because he guessed its name: it is rw-r--r--, and he has x on the directory. Hiding the names does not protect the content; only the permissions of the file do. The teacher can delete dave.txt: the owner of the directory may delete any file in it, even with the sticky bit; carol gets Permission denied for everything. → r, w and x · The Sticky Bit Setuid programs and scripts: Find the programs of the system that run as their owner, and show why the setuid bit works for programs but not for scripts. list all the setuid files in /usr, in the format of ls -l, without the errors, and count them; as root, copy /usr/bin/id to /srv/exam/rootid, and give it the setuid bit and rwxr-xr-x; run it as yourself and as bob; as root, create the script /srv/exam/rootid.sh, with the two lines #!/bin/bash and id, with the same permissions; run it as yourself; create /tmp/cap.txt, and give it the setuid bit without x for the owner; create the directory /tmp/capdir with rwxrwx--- and the sticky bit, with one number; print the permissions of both, as letters and as numbers; explain why /usr/bin/sudo is ---s--x--x on Fedora, and what -rwsr-xr-x on Ubuntu allows in addition; delete rootid, rootid.sh, cap.txt and capdir. 💡 man find: search for -perm and for -ls. Check: there are a few tens of setuid programs at most, all owned by root. rootid prints uid=1000(student) gid=1000(student) euid=0(root) ... (and uid= of bob for bob): id shows euid when the effective UID is not the real one. The script prints only uid=1000(student) ..., without euid: the kernel ignores the setuid bit on scripts. cap.txt is -rwSr--r-- (4644; Ubuntu: -rwSrw-r--, 4664) and capdir is drwxrwx--T (1770): a capital letter means that the bit is set, but the x under it is not. On Fedora, everybody may run sudo, as root, but nobody may read the file; on Ubuntu, everybody may also read it, and so copy it. → setuid · Special Permissions The UID is what matters: Show that a file belongs to a UID, not to a name, and what happens when a UID is used again. find the UID of carol, then delete her without her home directory; list /home with names, then with numbers; create the user grace, without a home directory, with the UID that carol had; list /home again, then delete grace and /home/carol. 💡 man ls: search for numeric; man useradd: search for uid and for no-create-home. Check: after carol is deleted, /home/carol shows numbers instead of an owner and a group: the files keep only the UID and the GID. When grace gets this UID, ls -l shows her as the owner of all the files of carol, and she may read and change them. Before a UID is used again, the files of the old user must be deleted or given to somebody else. → Users · chown and chgrp

Use the last 5 minutes of the lab to answer these questions together with your colleagues and the teaching assistant. There are no wrong answers for the last two. What is a user for the kernel? And a group? Where are the local users, groups and passwords kept? Which command do you use to look up a user? Why can everyone read /etc/passwd, but only root can read /etc/shadow? How does login check a password if the password is not stored anywhere? Which one set of permissions does the kernel use for you, when you open a file? Why can the owner of a file with ----rw---- not read it? What is the difference between sudo and su? Why does sudo work for student, but not for a new user? Why does sudo echo text > /etc/hosts fail? What do r, w and x mean for a directory? Why can you delete a file that you cannot write? Why can you not trust the prompt to tell you who you are? What surprised you most about the permissions today? Which permissions will you give to your own files from now on?

In the fifth lab you learned which user runs every program, and who may read and write every file. In this lab you will work with what is inside most of these files: text. You will meet the filters, small commands that read lines and write lines: cat, head, tail and sort work with whole lines, grep finds the lines that match a regular expression, cut, tr and sed change the inside of every line, and wc and awk count and compute. You will join them into pipelines that answer a question in one line, find out if a command worked from its exit code, and chain commands with && and ||. At the end, you will meet the three kinds of terminal editors, nano, vim and emacs, and start learning one of them. The most important idea of this lab is that text is the common language of the commands. Every filter reads lines of text, does one small thing with them, and writes lines of text, so the output of any filter can be the input of any other one. Pipes join filters into a pipeline: each command hands its text to the next one, a step closer to the answer, and the last one prints it. Besides its text, every command also gives back a number, its exit code, which tells the shell if it worked.

Understand what a filter is, and build a pipeline of filters that answers a question Show, reverse and cut out lines with cat, tac, head and tail Sort lines with sort, as text, as numbers and by a field, and count the repeated lines with uniq Write regular expressions, basic and extended, and search with them with grep Cut fields and characters out of every line with cut, and reverse or number the lines with rev and nl Change, delete and squeeze characters with tr, and replace text with sed Count lines, words and characters with wc, and compute sums and averages with awk Find out if a command worked from its exit code, and chain commands with && and || Edit a text file in the terminal with nano and with vim, start learning vim, nvim, hx or emacs, and choose the editor that other programs open with EDITOR
