The lab computers run Fedora with Sway, and the examples come from them. At home you may also use Ubuntu: the commands of this lab are the same, with a few differences: Fedora Ubuntu the prompt [student@fedora ~]$ student@ubuntu:~$ the program behind awk GNU awk (gawk) mawk, a smaller awk: this lab works the same on it vim and vimtutor if missing: sudo dnf install vim-enhanced if missing: sudo apt install vim install Helix (hx) sudo dnf install helix sudo snap install --classic helix install jq sudo dnf install jq sudo apt install jq EDITOR /usr/bin/nano not set: each program picks its own editor

A filter is a command that reads text, does one job with it, and writes the result to its standard output. It reads the files that it gets as parameters or, when it gets none, its standard input. In Pipes in lab 03 you joined a few of them with |: sort fruits.txt | uniq -c. A chain of commands joined by pipes is a pipeline. Think of an assembly line in a factory: every worker does one small job on the piece, and passes it on. A filter does not know what is before it or after it: only its input and its output. The filters of this lab do four kinds of jobs, and a typical pipeline uses them in this order: Kind What it does Commands line filters chooses which lines to keep, and their order cat, tac, head, tail, sort, uniq search keeps the lines that match a pattern grep change text changes what is inside every line cut, tr, sed, rev, nl compute turns the lines into a count, a sum, ... wc, uniq -c, awk [student@fedora lab06]$ grep ' 404$' access.log | cut -d' ' -f1 | sort | uniq -c 2 10.0.0.3 3 10.0.0.9 grep kept the lines that end with 404, the requests for pages that do not exist; cut kept only the first field, the address; sort | uniq -c counted every address. Each command is explained in the sections below. tip Build a pipeline one command at a time Run the first command and look at its output. Then press ↑, add | and the next command, and look again: each step should bring the text a little closer to the answer. While you work, add | head at the end to see only the first lines of a long output, and remove it when you are done. info "Write programs that do one thing and do it well. Write programs to work together. Write programs to handle text streams, because that is a universal interface." (Doug McIlroy, the inventor of the Unix pipe) All the commands of a pipeline run at the same time, each one in its own process, and the text flows between them while they run. The exercises at home and the challenges need the details: they are in How a Pipeline Runs.

The line filters work with whole lines: they choose which lines to keep and in which order, but do not change them. The examples use the files that exercise 1 creates in ~/lab06; fruits.txt has 7 lines: banana, apple, cherry, apple, kiwi, banana and apple.

You met cat in lab 02. Its options show what you cannot see in the text: Command What it does cat <FILE>... prints the files, one after another (concatenate) cat with no file, prints what it reads from the keyboard, until Ctrl+D cat -n <FILE> numbers every line cat -A <FILE> shows the invisible characters: a tab as ^I, the end of every line as $ tac <FILE> prints the lines in the reverse order, the last one first [student@fedora lab06]$ tac fruits.txt apple banana kiwi apple cherry apple banana [student@fedora lab06]$ printf 'a\tb \n' | cat -A a^Ib $ tac printed the same 7 lines, from the last one to the first one. cat -A showed the tab between a and b, and the space at the end of the line, before the $.
documents.s: Showing a File: cat and tac

documents.t: Command What it prints head -n <N> <FILE> the first N lines; without -n, the first 10 head -n -<N> <FILE> all the lines, except the last N lines; tail -n <N> <FILE> the last N lines; without -n, the last 10 tail -n +<N> <FILE> the lines from line N to the end: -n +2 skips only the first line tail -f <FILE> the last lines, then every new line written to the file, until Ctrl+C (follow) [student@fedora lab06]$ head -n 3 fruits.txt banana apple cherry [student@fedora lab06]$ head -n 5 fruits.txt | tail -n 1 kiwi [student@fedora lab06]$ tail -n +2 students.csv Alice,30,Paris Bob,25,London Carol,22,Bucharest head -n 5 | tail -n 1 kept the first 5 lines, then the last of them: the 5th line. tail -n +2 skipped the first line of students.csv, the header with the names of the columns. tip tail -f is how administrators watch a log, a file where a program adds a line for everything it does. Leave it running in a terminal, and you see every new line the moment it is written.
documents.s: The First and the Last Lines: head and tail

documents.t: sort prints the lines in alphabetical order. The options change what it compares: Option What it does -r in the reverse order -n compares the lines as numbers: 9 before 10 -u prints every line only once (unique) -t <C> the fields are separated by the character C (the default: spaces) -k <N>,<N> sorts by field N only; -k 2,2n: by field 2, as a number; -k 2: from field 2 to the end [student@fedora lab06]$ sort numbers.txt 10 100 2 9 [student@fedora lab06]$ sort -n numbers.txt 2 9 10 100 [student@fedora lab06]$ sort -t, -k 2,2n students.csv name,age,city Carol,22,Bucharest Bob,25,London Alice,30,Paris Without -n, sort compared the numbers as text, character by character: 100 came before 2, because 1 is before 2. -t, -k 2,2n sorted the lines of students.csv by the second field, the age, as a number. The header has no number in that field, so it counts as 0 and stays first. caution Without -n, numbers are sorted as text: 100 before 2. Use -n whenever the lines start with a number, or -k with n when the number is in another field.

You met uniq in Repeated Lines in lab 03: it compares a line only with the line right above it, so it comes after sort. Together with sort -nr and head, it finds the most frequent lines: [student@fedora lab06]$ sort fruits.txt | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -n 2 3 apple 2 banana sort | uniq -c counted every fruit, sort -nr put the largest count first, and head -n 2 kept the top two. Option What it prints uniq -c every line once, with how many times it appears uniq -d only the lines that appear more than once uniq -u only the lines that appear exactly once

A regular expression (regex) is a pattern that describes some text. For example, c.l means "a c, then any character, then an l": it matches col in color and cal in call. Most programs that search text understand regular expressions: grep, sed and awk, the search with / in less, man and vim, and almost every programming language. Think of a description of a person that you give to a friend at the station: you do not know the name, but "tall, with a red hat" finds the right person in the crowd. A regex finds the lines that match the description. grep '<REGEX>' <FILE> prints the lines that contain a match of the regex. The examples use words.txt: color colour cat category concatenate dog banana bat orange gal goal gooooal Cat UPB x86 notes.txt 2026-10-04 call 0722 123 456 caution A regex is not a glob The * of a glob (see Globbing in lab 04) means "any characters"; in a regex, * means "the previous item, any number of times", and "any characters" is .*. Always put the regex between single quotes: without them, the shell may expand it as a glob, before grep starts. If the current directory has a file banana.txt, grep ba* fruits.txt becomes grep banana.txt fruits.txt.

Regex Matches (It means) Example Matches in words.txt (Lines of words.txt it matches) abc the text abc, anywhere in the line cat cat, category, concatenate . any single character c.l color, colour, call ... ^ the start of the line ^ca cat, category, call ... $ the end of the line r$ color, colour [abc] one of the characters inside (a class) [0-9] x86, 2026-10-04, call ... [^abc] one character that is not inside; ^ means not only right after [ ^[^c] every line that does not start with c * the previous item, 0 or more times go*al gal, goal, gooooal .* any characters, or none ^c.*e$ concatenate \ the next character is plain text: \. is a real dot \. notes.txt [student@fedora lab06]$ grep 'go*al' words.txt gal goal gooooal [student@fedora lab06]$ grep '^[a-z]*$' words.txt | wc -l 12 [student@fedora lab06]$ grep '.' words.txt | wc -l 18 [student@fedora lab06]$ grep '\.' words.txt notes.txt go*al matched a g, any number of o, even none, then al. ^[a-z]*$ matched the lines that have only lowercase letters, from the start to the end: 12 of them. . alone matched every line that is not empty; \. matched only the line with a real dot.

With grep -E, five more characters are special: +, ?, { }, ( ) and |, and they make the regex shorter. The table also shows \b, which GNU grep understands with or without -E: Regex Matches Example Matches in words.txt + the previous item, 1 or more times [0-9]+ x86, 2026-10-04, call ... ? the previous item, 0 or 1 time: it is optional colou?r color, colour {n} the previous item, exactly n times; {n,m}: n to m [0-9]{4} 2026-10-04, call 0722 ... ( ) a group, repeated as one item b(an)*a banana, bat | one of the alternatives (or) cat|dog cat, category, concatenate, dog \b a word edge: the start or the end of a word \bcat\b only cat [student@fedora lab06]$ grep -E 'colou?r' words.txt color colour [student@fedora lab06]$ grep -E '^[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}$' words.txt 2026-10-04 [student@fedora lab06]$ grep -E '\b[0-9]{3}\b' words.txt call 0722 123 456 ^[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}$ matched a line that is only a date: 4 digits, -, 2 digits, -, 2 digits. \b[0-9]{3}\b matched a number of exactly 3 digits, 123; without the \b, it would match inside 0722 and 2026 too. info Without -E, grep uses the basic regular expressions, where +, ?, {, ( and | are plain characters (\+, \?, ... are special instead). Use -E whenever you need one of them. The whole list is in man 7 regex. tip A playground for regular expressions regex101.com colors the matches while you type the regex, and explains every part of it in plain words. Paste words.txt as the test string and keep the m flag on, so that ^ and $ match at every line, as in grep. Its default flavor, PCRE2, understands all the regular expressions of this lab; check the final one with grep anyway.

Option What it does -E uses the extended regular expressions -i ignores upper and lower case -v prints the lines that do not match -n prints the number of every line in front of it -c prints only the number of matching lines; a line with two matches counts once -o prints only the matching part, every match on its own line -w matches only whole words, like \b...\b around the regex -q prints nothing (quiet): the answer is in its exit code (see Exit Codes) -r searches all the files of a directory, and of its subdirectories [student@fedora lab06]$ grep -n 'an' fruits.txt 1:banana 6:banana [student@fedora lab06]$ grep -o -E '[0-9]+' words.txt 86 2026 10 04 0722 123 456 [student@fedora lab06]$ grep -v -c 'apple' fruits.txt 4 -n showed that banana is on the lines 1 and 6. -o printed every number of words.txt on its own line, without the rest of the line. -v -c counted the lines that do not contain apple.

Many text files are tables: every line is a row, and a character, the delimiter, splits it into fields, the columns. The fields are numbered from 1. File A line The delimiter a CSV file (comma-separated values) Alice,30,Paris , /etc/passwd (lab 05) student:x:1000:1000:Student:/home/student:/bin/bash : a log file, access.log 10.0.0.9 GET /logo.png 404 a space many programs the fields are aligned in columns a tab caution Every delimiter splits. In Bob 25 London, with three spaces after Bob, there are two empty fields between the spaces, and 25 is field 4, not 2.

Command What it prints cut -d<C> -f<N> <FILE> field N of every line; the fields are separated by the character C cut -d<C> -f1,3 fields 1 and 3, separated by the same C, in the order of the line: -f3,1 also prints field 1 first cut -d<C> -f2-4, -f2- fields 2 to 4; from field 2 to the end cut -f<N> without -d, the delimiter is the tab; a line with no tab is printed whole, whatever N is cut -c<N>-<M> <FILE> the characters N to M of every line, counted from 1 [student@fedora lab06]$ cut -d, -f1 students.csv name Alice Bob Carol [student@fedora lab06]$ cut -d, -f2- students.csv age,city 30,Paris 25,London 22,Bucharest [student@fedora lab06]$ cut -d' ' -f2 people.txt 30 9 102 47 -d, -f1 printed the first field, the names; -f2- printed everything from the second field on. The second line of people.txt is Bob 25 London: for Bob, field 2 is the empty field between the first two spaces, so cut printed an empty line. tr, in the next section, fixes it.

tr (translate) changes single characters, not words. It reads only its standard input: give it a file with < or with a pipe. Command What it does Example tr <SET1> <SET2> changes every character of SET1 into the character at the same position in SET2 tr abc xyz: cab → zxy tr -d <SET> deletes every character of SET tr -d a: banana → bnn tr -s <SET> squeezes a run of the same character of SET into one tr -s o: gooooal → goal A set is a list of characters, aeiou, or a range, a-z, 0-9; '
' is the end of a line and '	' a tab. [student@fedora lab06]$ tr a-z A-Z < fruits.txt | head -n 2 BANANA APPLE [student@fedora lab06]$ echo 'call 0722 123 456' | tr -d 0-9 call [student@fedora lab06]$ tr -s ' ' < people.txt | cut -d' ' -f2 30 25 9 102 47 [student@fedora lab06]$ echo "$PATH" | tr : '
' /home/student/.local/bin /home/student/bin /usr/local/bin /usr/bin ... a-z and A-Z have the same length: a became A, b became B, and so on. -d 0-9 deleted the digits; the spaces stayed. tr -s ' ' left one space between the fields of people.txt, so cut found the age of Bob in field 2. tr : '
' put every directory of PATH (lab 04) on its own line.

sed (stream editor) changes the text as it passes through, like a worker on the assembly line: it reads a line, changes it, prints it, and goes on to the next one. The file itself does not change. Unlike tr, sed works with words and regular expressions, not with single characters. Its most used command is s (substitute), which replaces the text that a regex matches: sed 's/<REGEX>/<NEW TEXT>/<FLAGS>' <FILE> Written as What it does s/apple/pear/ replaces the first match of every line s/apple/pear/g replaces every match of the line (global) s/apple/pear/gi the same, ignoring upper and lower case sed -E 's/...//' the regex is an extended one, as for grep -E s/apple//g the new text is empty: deletes the matches s|/usr|/opt| any character can separate the parts: useful when the text has / [student@fedora lab06]$ echo 'apple and apple pie' | sed 's/apple/pear/' pear and apple pie [student@fedora lab06]$ echo 'apple and apple pie' | sed 's/apple/pear/g' pear and pear pie [student@fedora lab06]$ echo 'call 0722 123 456' | sed -E 's/[0-9]+/N/g' call N N N [student@fedora lab06]$ sed 's/,/ /g' students.csv name age city Alice 30 Paris Bob 25 London Carol 22 Bucharest Without g, only the first apple changed. [0-9]+ matched each number, and every match became N. sed printed the changed text; students.csv itself did not change. danger sed -i writes the result back into the file, instead of printing it. There is no undo: run the command without -i first, and look at the output.

Command What it does rev <FILE> reverses the characters of every line; the order of the lines stays (that is tac) nl <FILE> adds a first column with the number of the line, and a tab; empty lines get no number [student@fedora lab06]$ rev fruits.txt | head -n 2 ananab elppa [student@fedora lab06]$ echo /usr/share/doc/bash | rev | cut -d/ -f1 | rev bash cut cannot count fields from the end. rev put the last field first, cut -f1 took it, and the second rev turned it back.
documents.s: Reversing and Numbering: rev and nl

documents.t: wc (word count) counts the lines, the words and the bytes: Option What it counts -l the lines -w the words: the groups of characters separated by spaces -c the bytes -m the characters: a letter like ș takes 2 bytes, but it is 1 character [student@fedora lab06]$ wc fruits.txt 7 7 44 fruits.txt [student@fedora lab06]$ wc -l < fruits.txt 7 [student@fedora lab06]$ echo 'mașină' | wc -c -m 7 9 Without options, wc printed the lines, the words and the bytes, then the name of the file. With <, wc did not know the name of the file (see Input in lab 03): it printed only the number. mașină and the end of the line are 7 characters, but 9 bytes: ș and ă take two bytes each.

awk is a small programming language for tables. An awk program is a list of conditions, each with an action between { }: for every line, awk splits it into fields and runs the action of every condition that is true for the line. A condition is optional; END is a condition that is true once, after the last line. Written as What it is -F, the delimiter is ,; without -F, any run of spaces and tabs $1, $2, ..., $NF the fields; $NF is the last one, not to be confused with NF; $0 is the whole line NF, NR the number of fields of the line; the number of the line, from 1 ==, !=, <, >=, ... compare two values: numbers as numbers, text as text; text goes between ": $2 == "apple" ~ /regex/, !~ /regex/ matches, does not match a regex &&, ||, ! and, or, not { print $1, $3 } prints fields 1 and 3, separated by a space; print $1 $3, without the ,, prints alice3 { s += $3; n++ } adds field 3 to the variable s, and adds 1 to n; variables start at 0 The examples use orders.csv, a header and 6 orders: name,fruit,count alice,apple,3 bob,kiwi,1 carol,apple,2 alice,banana,5 dan,apple,1 alice,apple,2 [student@fedora lab06]$ awk -F, '{ s += $3 } END { print s }' orders.csv 14 [student@fedora lab06]$ awk -F, 'NR > 1 { s += $3; n++ } END { print s / n }' orders.csv 2.33333 [student@fedora lab06]$ awk -F, '$2 == "apple" { s += $3 } END { print s }' orders.csv 8 [student@fedora lab06]$ awk -F, '$2 ~ /an/ { print $1, $2 }' orders.csv alice banana [student@fedora lab06]$ awk '{ print NF, $NF }' people.txt 3 Paris 3 London 3 Rome 3 Oslo 3 Madrid The first program added field 3 of every line, and printed the sum at the end; the header count is not a number, so it added 0. NR > 1 skipped the header, and n counted the orders: 14 / 6 = 2.33333. $2 == "apple" added only the apples; $2 ~ /an/ printed the orders whose fruit contains an. Without -F, awk split Bob 25 London at the run of spaces: 3 fields, no empty ones. tip Put the awk program between single quotes: $1 and $3 are for awk, not for the shell.

How many customers ordered apples? Build the pipeline one command at a time, and look at the text after every step: [student@fedora lab06]$ tail -n +2 orders.csv | grep ',apple,' alice,apple,3 carol,apple,2 dan,apple,1 alice,apple,2 [student@fedora lab06]$ tail -n +2 orders.csv | grep ',apple,' | cut -d, -f1 alice carol dan alice [student@fedora lab06]$ tail -n +2 orders.csv | grep ',apple,' | cut -d, -f1 | sort -u alice carol dan [student@fedora lab06]$ tail -n +2 orders.csv | grep ',apple,' | cut -d, -f1 | sort -u | wc -l 3 tail -n +2 skipped the header, and grep ',apple,' kept the orders of apples; the commas around apple skip a fruit like pineapple. cut kept the names; alice ordered apples twice, so sort -u kept every name once; wc -l counted them.

Every command ends with a number between 0 and 255, its exit code: 0 means success, any other number an error. The shell keeps the exit code of the last command in $? (see Special Parameters in lab 04). The manual page of a command says what its numbers mean, in the section EXIT STATUS: grep ends with When 0 it found at least one line 1 it found nothing 2 an error: for example, the file does not exist [student@fedora lab06]$ grep -q kiwi fruits.txt [student@fedora lab06]$ echo $? 0 [student@fedora lab06]$ grep -q mango fruits.txt [student@fedora lab06]$ echo $? 1 [student@fedora lab06]$ grep kiwi nope.txt grep: nope.txt: No such file or directory [student@fedora lab06]$ echo $? 2 grep -q printed nothing; its exit code said if it found kiwi, 0, or not, 1. Command What it does true nothing; it ends with 0 false nothing; it ends with 1 exit <N> ends the shell, or a script, with the exit code N A command killed by a signal (lab 04) ends with 128 plus the number of the signal: Ctrl+C (SIGINT, 2) gives 130.

Written as What it does a ; b runs a, then b, whether a worked or not; like two separate lines a && b runs b only if a ended with 0: "a, and then b" a || b runs b only if a did not end with 0: "a, or else b" [student@fedora lab06]$ grep -q kiwi fruits.txt && echo 'kiwi found' kiwi found [student@fedora lab06]$ grep -q mango fruits.txt && echo 'mango found' [student@fedora lab06]$ grep -q mango fruits.txt || echo 'no mango' no mango [student@fedora lab06]$ mkdir -p backup && cp fruits.txt backup/ && echo 'saved' saved && skipped echo 'mango found', because grep ended with 1; || ran echo 'no mango' for the same reason. cp ran only after mkdir worked, and echo only after cp worked. caution a && b || c is not "if a, then b, else c": the shell reads it from left to right, so c also runs when a works but b fails. It is safe when b cannot fail, like echo. a && b || c is not "if a, then b, else c". The shell reads it from left to right, and || looks at the exit code of the last command that ran before it: when a works, that is b. So c also runs when a works but b fails: true && false || echo C prints C. You can use a && b || c as "if a, then b, else c" only when b cannot fail, like echo: then c runs only when a fails.

The exit code of a pipeline is the exit code of its last command: [student@fedora lab06]$ cut -d, -f2 orders.csv | grep -q kiwi && echo 'kiwi ordered' || echo 'no kiwi' kiwi ordered [student@fedora lab06]$ cut -d, -f2 nope.csv | sort cut: nope.csv: No such file or directory [student@fedora lab06]$ echo $? 0 In the first line, grep -q found kiwi in the column of the fruits: the pipeline ended with 0. In the second, cut failed, but sort, the last command, worked: the pipeline ended with 0. The error message is on the screen, but $?, && and || see only the 0. How a Pipeline Runs shows how to catch the failure.
documents.s: The Exit Code of a Pipeline

documents.t: You edit text files all the time: settings in /etc and in ~/.config, programs, notes. On a server, over the network, or on a virtual terminal (lab 04), there is no window: you need an editor that runs inside the terminal. Terminal editors come in three kinds. In a simple editor, nano, what you type goes into the text. In a modal editor, vim, nvim or Helix (hx), the keys are commands, and you type text only in one of its modes. emacs is in between: what you type goes into the text, as in nano, but every command is a chord, keys held down together, and it can do almost anything. Think of it as a much more powerful nano.

You met nano in lab 02; it is the default editor of Fedora and Ubuntu. The bottom of the screen lists its keys: ^ means Ctrl and M- means Alt. All of them are in the nano tab of The Keys of Each Editor.

vim (Vi IMproved) is modal: the same key does different things in different modes. It starts in the Normal mode, where every key is a command: j does not type a j, it moves the cursor down, and x deletes a character. To type text, press i to enter the Insert mode; press Esc to go back to the Normal mode. It takes some time to get used to, but it is also the strength of vim: when you edit, you spend most of the time moving and changing text, not typing it, and in the Normal mode every letter is a command, with no Ctrl to hold. Mode What the keys do Enter it with The last line shows Normal move, delete, copy, paste Esc, from any other mode nothing Insert type text from Normal: i, a, o -- INSERT -- Command line type a command: save, quit, replace; Enter runs it : (or / to search) : (or /) and what you type Visual select text, then act on it: d deletes, y copies v (characters), V (lines) -- VISUAL --, -- VISUAL LINE -- vi, the ancestor of vim, is on every Unix system; nvim (Neovim) is a newer vim, with the same keys. Helix (hx) is modal too, but you select first, then act: x selects the line, then d deletes it (in vim, dd does both). Helix knows the programming languages without any settings. tip Lost in vim? Look at the last line to know the mode. Press Esc a few times to get back to the Normal mode, then type :q! and Enter to quit without saving. vimtutor teaches the rest in 30 minutes.

emacs(Editor MACroS) has no modes: what you type goes into the text. Every command is a chord: Ctrl+X Ctrl+S saves, Ctrl+X Ctrl+C quits. Its manual writes Ctrl as C- and Alt as M- (Meta): C-x C-s. Start it with emacs -nw (no window) to keep it in the terminal, and press Ctrl+G to cancel a command that you started by mistake.

The same actions in the four editors: choose the tab of the editor you use. nano vim / nvim hx emacs Action Keys open a file nano <FILE> type text type it save Ctrl+O (write out), then Enter to keep the name quit Ctrl+X; if the file changed, it asks to save: Y or N quit without saving Ctrl+X, then N cancel a command Ctrl+C undo, redo Alt+U, Alt+E search, the next match Ctrl+W (where is), Alt+W cut the line Ctrl+K copy the line Alt+6 paste Ctrl+U the first line, the last line Alt+\, Alt+/ go to a line, by its number Ctrl+_ replace Ctrl+\ the tutorial none: the bottom of the screen lists the keys Action Keys open a file vim <FILE>, nvim <FILE> type text i (the Insert mode), then Esc back to the Normal mode save :w quit :q; :wq saves and quits quit without saving :q! cancel a command Esc undo, redo u, Ctrl+R search, the next match /text Enter, n cut the line dd copy the line yy (yank) paste p, below the current line the first line, the last line gg, G go to a line, by its number :42 goes to line 42 replace :%s/old/new/g, like sed: old is a regex, % means all the lines the tutorial vimtutor; in nvim, :Tutor More keys of the Normal mode: Keys Action h j k l, or the arrows left, down, up, right w, b the next word, the previous word 0, $ the start, the end of the line a the Insert mode, after the cursor o, O a new line below, above, in Insert mode x delete a character A number in front of a command repeats it: 5j goes 5 lines down, 3dd deletes 3 lines. The keys h j k l are the ones of Sway, from lab 01. Action Keys open a file hx <FILE> type text i (the Insert mode), then Esc back to the Normal mode save :w quit :q; :wq saves and quits quit without saving :q! cancel a command Esc undo, redo u, U search, the next match /text Enter, n cut the line x selects the line, d cuts it copy the line x, then y paste p, after the selection the first line, the last line gg, ge go to a line, by its number :goto 42 replace % selects the file, sold Enter selects every match, cnew Esc changes them the tutorial hx --tutor After g or Space, Helix shows a menu with the keys that can follow. Action Keys open a file emacs -nw <FILE> type text type it save Ctrl+X Ctrl+S quit Ctrl+X Ctrl+C quit without saving Ctrl+X Ctrl+C, then n and yes cancel a command Ctrl+G undo, redo Ctrl+/; to redo, Ctrl+G, then Ctrl+/ search, the next match Ctrl+S, then Ctrl+S again cut the line Ctrl+A (the start of the line), then Ctrl+K twice copy the line cut it, then Ctrl+Y pastes it back; the next Ctrl+Y pastes a copy paste Ctrl+Y (yank) the first line, the last line Alt+<, Alt+> go to a line, by its number Alt+G G, then the number replace Alt+% old Enter new Enter, then ! replaces all the next matches the tutorial Ctrl+H T

Some programs open an editor for you, on a temporary file: they wait until you save and quit, then read what you wrote. To know which editor to start, they read the environment variable EDITOR (Environment Variables in lab 04). A few of them look first at VISUAL, an older name for the same choice: if it is set, it wins. Program What it opens in the editor bash, the keys Ctrl+X Ctrl+E the command you are typing; bash runs it when the editor quits less, the key v the file you are reading sudoedit <FILE> a copy of a system file, put back in place when the editor quits crontab -e the list of the commands that run on a schedule git commit the message of the commit [student@fedora ~]$ echo "[$EDITOR] [$VISUAL]" [/usr/bin/nano] [] [student@fedora ~]$ export EDITOR=vim [student@fedora ~]$ echo 'export EDITOR=vim' >> ~/.bashrc echo showed that Fedora chose nano, and that VISUAL is empty (Ubuntu: both are empty, and each program picks its own editor). export EDITOR=vim chose vim for the programs started from this terminal, until you close it. echo ... >> ~/.bashrc added the same line at the end of ~/.bashrc (the settings of bash, read by every new terminal). caution Use >>, not >: > ~/.bashrc replaces the whole file with that one line, and the settings that were in it are lost.

note Going deeper You do not need this section for the exercises of the lab, the 🧪 First Steps. Read it at home: the 🏠 Going Further exercises and the 📝 Challenges use it. For a pipeline, the shell starts every command at the same time, each as a child process, and joins them with pipes. A pipe is a small buffer in the kernel: the output (1) of a command writes into it, and the input (0) of the next command reads from it. Think of a tube between two workers: the first one drops pieces in at one end, the second takes them out at the other. What happens The result the pipe is empty, and the next command wants to read it waits until there is text the pipe is full (64 KiB) the writer waits until the reader takes some text out the writer ends the reader gets the end of file, and can finish the reader ends before the writer at its next write, the writer gets the signal SIGPIPE (13), and ends Ctrl+C, Ctrl+Z they go to all the commands: the pipeline is one job (lab 04) [student@fedora lab06]$ yes | head -n 3 y y y [student@fedora lab06]$ echo "${PIPESTATUS[@]}" 141 0 yes prints y without end; head ended after 3 lines, and yes got SIGPIPE at its next write: 128 + 13 = 141. PIPESTATUS is a variable of bash with the exit codes of every command of the last pipeline; $? has only the last one. The pipes of a process are in its directory in /proc (see The /proc File System in lab 03): readlink /proc/<PID>/fd/1 prints pipe:[48211] when output 1 goes to a pipe; both ends of the same pipe have the same number. Setting What it does set -o pipefail the exit code of a pipeline is the one of the rightmost command that failed, or 0 if none failed; set +o pipefail turns it off grep --line-buffered grep writes every line at once; without it, when its output is a pipe, it waits until it has 4 KiB of text [student@fedora lab06]$ set -o pipefail [student@fedora lab06]$ cut -d, -f2 nope.csv | sort cut: nope.csv: No such file or directory [student@fedora lab06]$ echo $? 1 [student@fedora lab06]$ set +o pipefail With pipefail, the failure of cut was not hidden any more: the pipeline ended with 1.

Problem Solution A command waits, and the prompt does not come back It reads the keyboard: you forgot the file, or the <. Press Ctrl+D or Ctrl+C tr: extra operand ‘fruits.txt’ tr reads only its input: tr a-z A-Z < fruits.txt sort puts 100 before 2 It sorts as text: add -n, or n after -k uniq leaves repeated lines They are not next to each other: sort first cut prints empty lines, or the wrong field There are several delimiters in a row: squeeze them with tr -s, or use awk cut -f2 prints the whole line Without -d, the delimiter is the tab, and the line has none: give the delimiter with -d cut: the delimiter must be a single character -d takes one character: -d,, -d' ', -d: grep finds lines that you did not expect . and * are special in a regex: write \. for a real dot, \* for a real star grep: warning: stray \ before d \d is not a digit in grep: use [0-9] grep -E 'a+' works but grep 'a+' finds nothing In basic regexes, + is a plain character: use -E grep with * finds strange results, or the wrong files The regex is not between single quotes, and the shell expanded it as a glob sed: -e expression #1, char 8: unknown option to `s' The text has a /: use another separator, s|/usr|/opt| awk -F, '{ print $2 }' prints empty lines The delimiter is wrong: look at a line with cat -A, and give the right one with -F awk "{ print $1 }" prints whole lines Between double quotes, the shell replaced $1 with nothing: use single quotes vim writes letters in strange places, or does not type You are in the wrong mode: press Esc, then i to type E37: No write since last change (add ! to override) vim does not quit without saving: :wq saves, :q! throws the changes away vim: command not found Use vi, or install vim-enhanced (Ubuntu: vim) jq: error ... Cannot index array with "city" The file is a list: take its elements first, .[] | .city

🧪 First Steps (exercises 1 - 14): one idea at a time, in the order of the lab, to do in the lab; 🏠 Going Further (exercises 15 - 34): longer exercises, to do at home; some of them look at how the commands of a pipeline run together, explained in How a Pipeline Runs; 📝 Challenges (exercises 35 - 41): the hardest ones, like the ones at the exam. danger The filters only print: the files change only with >, sed -i or an editor. Before you write the result over a file, look at it on the screen, and never redirect the output of a command into its own input file: sort f.txt > f.txt leaves f.txt empty, because the shell empties the file for > before sort starts reading it.

Do these exercises in order, during the lab. Each one starts with what it wants you to achieve, and tries one idea from the lab: read the section linked under its goal if you get stuck. Run the commands in ~/lab06, unless the exercise says otherwise. The practice tree: Create the files that the other exercises use, in ~/lab06. run these commands (copy them from the browser with Ctrl+C and paste them in the terminal with Ctrl+Shift+V): mkdir -p ~/lab06 cd ~/lab06 printf '%s
' banana apple cherry apple kiwi banana apple > fruits.txt printf '%s
' 10 9 100 2 > numbers.txt printf '%s
' color colour cat category concatenate dog banana bat orange \ gal goal gooooal Cat UPB x86 notes.txt 2026-10-04 'call 0722 123 456' > words.txt printf '%s
' name,age,city Alice,30,Paris Bob,25,London Carol,22,Bucharest > students.csv printf '%s
' 'Alice 30 Paris' 'Bob 25 London' 'Carol 9 Rome' 'Dave 102 Oslo' 'Erin 47 Madrid' > people.txt printf '%s
' name,fruit,count alice,apple,3 bob,kiwi,1 carol,apple,2 \ alice,banana,5 dan,apple,1 alice,apple,2 > orders.csv cat > access.log << 'END' 10.0.0.7 GET /index.html 200 10.0.0.9 GET /logo.png 404 10.0.0.7 GET /about.html 200 10.0.0.3 GET /old.html 404 10.0.0.9 GET /favicon.ico 404 10.0.0.5 GET /index.html 200 10.0.0.9 GET /admin 404 10.0.0.3 GET /old.html 404 END list the files of ~/lab06. Check The commands print nothing. access.log, fruits.txt, numbers.txt, orders.csv, people.txt, students.csv and words.txt. Line filters Both ends of a file: Look at parts of a file, without printing all of it. → Showing a File · The First and the Last Lines print fruits.txt with the number of every line; then print it from the last line to the first; print only the 5th line of fruits.txt; print students.csv without its header; create the empty file live.log; in a second terminal, follow it; in the first terminal, add the line first to it; stop following it. Hint man cat: search for number; man tail: search for +NUM and for follow; add a line with echo and >> (lab 03). Check The lines are numbered 1 to 7; from the last line, the file starts with apple and ends with banana. kiwi. The output starts with Alice,30,Paris. first appears in the second terminal the moment you add it. Sort and count: Put lines in the right order, and find the lines that repeat. → Sorting: sort · Counting Repeated Lines sort numbers.txt as text, then as numbers, then as numbers from the largest; print the students of students.csv, without the header, from the oldest to the youngest; print every fruit of fruits.txt once, then only the fruits that appear exactly once; print the most frequent fruit, with how many times it appears, with one pipeline. Hint man sort: search for field-separator and for KEYDEF; man uniq: search for unique. Check 10 100 2 9, then 2 9 10 100, then 100 10 9 2. Alice, Bob, Carol. apple, banana, cherry and kiwi; then only cherry and kiwi. 3 apple. Why: as text, 100 comes before 2 because 1 comes before 2, whatever follows it. Regular expressions Regular expressions: Describe lines with a pattern, find them in words.txt, and see why a regex needs quotes. → Basic Regular Expressions · Extended Regular Expressions · Regular Expressions For steps 1 - 4, first write the regex on paper, then check it with grep: find the lines that end with l; find the lines that have exactly three characters, all of them lowercase letters; find the lines that have a g, one or more o, then al; find the lines that are exactly cat or exactly dog; create the empty file cat.txt; first guess what grep ca* words.txt and grep 'ca*' words.txt print, then run them; delete cat.txt. Hint The tables of Basic Regular Expressions and Extended Regular Expressions; for step 2, think of ^ and $. For step 5, print the words that grep receives with echo grep ca* words.txt. Check gal, goal, gooooal. cat, dog, bat, gal, but not Cat, UPB or x86. goal and gooooal, but not gal. cat and dog, but not category. grep ca* words.txt prints nothing; grep 'ca*' words.txt prints color, colour, cat, category, concatenate and call 0722 123 456. Why: without quotes, the shell turned ca* into cat.txt, and grep searched for the text cat.txt; with quotes, grep got ca*, a c and any number of a, even none. grep options: Make grep print exactly what you need: other lines, the line numbers, or only a number. → grep Options print the settings of /etc/login.defs (lab 05), without the comments (the lines that start with #) and without the empty lines; then count them; print the line of the UMASK setting, with its line number; count the lines of words.txt that contain cat; then print only those where cat is a whole word, in lowercase or in capital letters. Hint man grep: search for invert, line-number, word-regexp and ignore-case; an empty line is ^$. Check Lines like UID_MIN 1000, a few dozen of them. One line, with its number and a : in front: UMASK is 022. 3; then cat and Cat. Change text Columns and characters: Keep only some fields of every line with cut, and change characters with tr. → Cutting Columns: cut · Changing Characters: tr print the names and the cities of students.csv, without the header; print the name and the shell of every user, from the users database; print fruits.txt in capital letters; then print the fruits without their vowels; print the age of every person in people.txt, with tr and cut; then print the people from the youngest to the oldest; print the directories of your PATH, one per line. Hint man cut: search for delimiter and fields; /etc/passwd has 7 fields, separated by :, and getent passwd prints all the users (lab 05). man tr: search for delete and squeeze; tr reads only its input. Check Alice,Paris, Bob,London, Carol,Bucharest. Lines like student:/bin/bash. BANANA, APPLE, CHERRY, ...; then bnn, ppl, chrry, ppl, kw, bnn, ppl. 30, 25, 9, 102, 47; then Carol, Bob, Alice, Erin, Dave. One directory per line, among them /usr/bin. Why: for cut, every space is a delimiter, so tr -s ' ' must squeeze the spaces of Bob 25 first; sorted as text, Dave (102) would come first and Carol (9) last. Replace text: Change words and parts of lines with sed, without changing the files. → Replacing Text: sed · Reversing and Numbering replace apple with pear in fruits.txt; then check that fruits.txt did not change; print students.csv with tabs instead of commas, then cut its second column without -d; print the line notes.txt of words.txt without its extension; print your home directory with /home replaced by /users; then print only the name of the current directory, with pwd, rev and cut. Hint Replacing Text: sed; 	 is a tab; for step 4, use another separator than /, and remember that cut cannot count the fields from the end. Check pear three times; fruits.txt still has apple. age, 30, 25, 22. notes. /users/student; then lab06. Counting and computing Count and compute: Count the lines and the characters of a text with wc, and answer questions about the orders of orders.csv with awk. → Counting: wc · Computing: awk count the lines, the words and the bytes of words.txt; then only its lines, without the name of the file; count the characters and the bytes of Iași; compute how many fruits alice ordered in total; compute the average count of the orders of apples; print the name and the UID of the users whose UID is at least 1000, from the users database. Hint man wc: search for chars. Computing: awk has all you need; the UID is field 3 of the users database. Check 18 21 128 words.txt, then 18. 5 characters, but 6 bytes. 10. 2. student 1000, and also nobody 65534. Why: Iași and the end of the line are 5 characters, but ș takes 2 bytes. A pipeline Read a log: Answer questions about the requests of access.log, with pipelines that you build one command at a time. → A Pipeline, Step by Step · Filters print how many times each page (the third field) was asked for, the most requested first, with its place in the ranking (1, 2, ...) in front; print the addresses that asked for a page that does not exist (status 404), each once; count the requests that ended with 404. Use the last 5 minutes of the lab to answer these questions together with your colleagues and the teaching assistant. There are no wrong answers for the last two. What is a filter? Why can the output of any filter be the input of any other one? Why does uniq need sort before it? Why does sort put 100 before 2, and how do you fix it? What is the difference between * in a glob and * in a regular expression? Why do you put a regex between single quotes? When do you use cut, and when awk? What happens to cut when the fields are separated by several spaces? What is the difference between tr and sed? What does the exit code 0 mean? What do && and || do with it? Which exit code does a pipeline have? What can it hide? How do you quit vim without saving? Which filter surprised you most today? Which editor will you use from now on, and why?

In the sixth lab you processed text with filters and edited text files with vim and nano. In the programming course you write programs in C, and the IDE builds and runs them when you press a button. In this lab you will build them yourself, in the terminal, and see what happens behind that button. You will see how a compiled language differs from an interpreted one, compile with gcc, and follow the four steps of the compilation pipeline: the preprocessor, the compiler, the assembler and the linker. You will split a program into modules, read the build errors of each step, and set up an editor that shows these errors while you type, through the language server clangd. Then you will let make build the program for you, from a Makefile: rules, automatic variables, pattern rules, phony targets and header dependencies. At the end, you will stop a running program with the debugger gdb, and save the versions of your project with git. The most important idea of this lab is that building a program is a chain of files: every file that you build (an object file, the executable) is made from other files (the sources, the headers, other object files) by one command. A Makefile writes this chain down as rules, and make compares the modification times of the files: it runs a command only when its result is missing, or older than one of the files it is made from.

Understand the difference between a compiled, an interpreted and a bytecode language Compile and run a C program in the terminal with gcc, without an IDE, and turn on the warnings with -Wall Follow the four steps of the compilation pipeline, and stop after each of them with gcc -E, -S and -c Look inside the files of each step with file, nm and ldd Split a program into modules (a .h and a .c file), compile every .c file to an object file, and link the object files into an executable Read a build error, find out which step reported it, and fix it Understand what a language server is and how an editor talks to it, and use clangd from an editor: errors, information, completion and go to definition Write a Makefile with rules, and understand how make decides what to build from the modification times Shorten a Makefile with automatic variables ($@, $<, $^), pattern rules and variables (CC, CFLAGS) Add the phony targets all, run and clean, and declare them with .PHONY Write the header dependencies on the right rules Build a program with debug information (-g), stop it with gdb and look at its variables Save the versions of a project with git init, git add, git commit, git status, git diff and git log

Software Development The manual pages: man gcc, man make, man file, man nm, man objdump, man ldd, man ar, man strip, man ld.so, man gdb, man git, man git-commit, man git-diff, man git-log, man git-restore, man gitignore, man git-push, man git-pull, man git-clone, man ssh-keygen, man bear and clangd --help

The lab computers run Fedora with Sway, and the examples come from them. At home you may also use Ubuntu: the commands are the same, with a few differences: Fedora Ubuntu install the tools of this lab sudo dnf install gcc make gdb git clang-tools-extra sudo apt install build-essential gdb git clangd a function called without a declaration an error (GCC 14 and newer) Ubuntu 24.04 has GCC 13: only a warning the C library, in the output of ldd /lib64/libc.so.6 /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6 the folder of cc1, a program that gcc runs /usr/libexec/gcc/x86_64-redhat-linux/<VERSION>/ /usr/lib/gcc/x86_64-linux-gnu/<VERSION>/ gcc -static (in Libraries) needs sudo dnf install glibc-static works gcc --version prints the version of gcc. The examples are for a PC (x86-64); on a computer with an ARM processor, such as a Mac with Apple silicon, the assembly code and the addresses look different.

The processor runs only machine code: instructions written as bytes, different for every family of processors (x86-64, ARM64, RISC-V). People write source code: text, in a programming language. Someone has to translate the source code into machine code, and the languages differ in who does it and when: Kind Who translates the source code When Examples compiled a compiler, into machine code: the result is an executable once, before the program runs C, C++, Rust, Go interpreted an interpreter, a program that reads the source and does what it says every time the program runs shell scripts (bash, sh) bytecode a compiler, into bytecode (machine code for an imaginary processor); a virtual machine runs it before the program runs (Java, C#), or when it starts (Python, JavaScript) Java, C#, Python, JavaScript Think of a book in a foreign language: a compiled program is a printed translation, made once and read many times; an interpreted program is read with a translator next to you, who translates every sentence while you read. [student@fedora lab07]$ ./hello.sh Hello from bash! [student@fedora lab07]$ file hello.sh /usr/bin/bash hello.sh: Bourne-Again shell script, ASCII text executable /usr/bin/bash: ELF 64-bit LSB pie executable, x86-64, ... hello.sh is text: the interpreter, bash, reads it line by line. bash itself is machine code, an ELF file (Executable and Linkable Format, the format of the programs on Linux), written in C and compiled. Compiled Interpreted speed fast: the processor runs the machine code directly slower: the interpreter translates the source at every run errors the compiler finds many of them before the program runs an error shows up only when its line runs after a change compile again, then run just run it again portability one executable for each processor and system the same file runs wherever the interpreter is installed info A language is not compiled or interpreted: the program that runs it is. python3 compiles a script to bytecode every time it starts, then its virtual machine runs the bytecode; only the modules that a script imports are kept compiled, in __pycache__. The virtual machines of Java and JavaScript also compile the code that runs often to machine code, while it runs: just in time (JIT).

gcc (the GNU Compiler Collection) is the C compiler of Linux, and often the one that runs behind the Build button of your IDE. The examples use hello.c, which exercise 1 creates in ~/lab07: ~/lab07/hello.c #include <stdio.h> #define TIMES 3 int main(void) { // say hello a few times for (int i = 0; i < TIMES; i++) { printf("Hello, %d!\n", i); } return 0; } [student@fedora lab07]$ gcc hello.c -o hello [student@fedora lab07]$ ./hello Hello, 0! Hello, 1! Hello, 2! gcc hello.c -o hello compiled hello.c into the executable hello; it printed nothing, because nothing went wrong. The program starts with ./: the current directory is not in PATH (see The PATH Search in lab 04). Option What it does -o <FILE> the name of the output file; without it, the executable is a.out -Wall turns on the warnings about code that is legal, but probably wrong -g adds the debug information, for gdb (see Debugging) -c, -S, -E stop after a step of the pipeline (see The Compilation Pipeline) -l<NAME> links the library <NAME>: -lm for the math functions, like sqrt -I <DIR> also looks for the header files in <DIR> -static creates a static executable (see The Linker) info Behind the button of the IDE The Build button of an IDE (Code::Blocks, Visual Studio Code, CLion) runs gcc with options like these, and Run starts the executable; the build log of the IDE shows the exact commands. In the terminal, no button builds the program before it runs: after you edit a .c file, you run gcc (or make) yourself. You write the C files with a text editor from Text Editors in lab 06; after Build Errors, you will set up one that understands C.

gcc hello.c -o hello looks like one step, but it is four. Each step reads the file of the step before, and writes a new file. An option stops gcc after a step, so you can look at that file: Step What it does Stop after it Writes preprocessor copies the #include files in, replaces the #defines, removes the comments gcc -E hello.c -o hello.i hello.i, preprocessed C compiler translates C into assembly, the text form of the machine code gcc -S hello.c hello.s, assembly assembler translates assembly into machine code gcc -c hello.c hello.o, object file linker joins the object files and the libraries into an executable gcc hello.o -o hello hello, executable Think of a car factory: the first station brings the parts together (the preprocessor), the next ones shape them (the compiler and the assembler), and the last one assembles the car (the linker). The Preprocessor: gcc -E​ The lines that start with # are for the preprocessor. It changes the text before the compiler sees it, a bit like sed, and does not check that the result is correct C. [student@fedora lab07]$ gcc -E hello.c -o hello.i [student@fedora lab07]$ wc -l hello.c hello.i 12 hello.c 825 hello.i 837 total [student@fedora lab07]$ grep 'int printf' hello.i extern int printf (const char *__restrict __format, ...); [student@fedora lab07]$ tail -n 8 hello.i int main(void) { for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { printf("Hello, %d!\n", i); } return 0; } #include <stdio.h> copied the whole file /usr/include/stdio.h (and the files that it includes) into hello.i: hundreds of lines, among them the declaration of printf. The number of lines depends on the version of the C library. #define TIMES 3 replaced TIMES with 3, and the comment is gone. #include <stdio.h>, with angle brackets, looks only in the folders of the system, like /usr/include; #include "lib.h", with quotes, looks first in the folder of the .c file. The Compiler: gcc -S​ The compiler translates C into assembly: one line for every instruction of the processor, still a text file. [student@fedora lab07]$ gcc -S hello.c [student@fedora lab07]$ grep -E 'call|cmpl|jle' hello.s call printf@PLT cmpl $2, -4(%rbp) jle .L3 The loop became a compare (cmpl, is i at most 2?) and a jump back (jle, jump if less or equal). printf is only called: its code is not in hello.s. Two options make hello.s easier to read: Option What it does -fverbose-asm writes each line of C as a comment above its instructions, and the variable that each one uses -masm=intel writes the Intel syntax instead of the AT&T syntax, the default of gcc (x86 only) [student@fedora lab07]$ gcc -S -fverbose-asm hello.c [student@fedora lab07]$ grep -B1 cmpl hello.s # hello.c:8: for (int i = 0; i < TIMES; i++) { cmpl $2, -4(%rbp) #, i [student@fedora lab07]$ gcc -S -masm=intel hello.c [student@fedora lab07]$ grep -E 'call|cmp|jle' hello.s call printf@PLT cmp DWORD PTR -4[rbp], 2 jle .L3 -fverbose-asm showed that the compare comes from line 8 of hello.c, the for, and that -4(%rbp) is i. -masm=intel wrote the same instructions in the Intel syntax, the one of the manuals of Intel and AMD and of most books: the operands are in the reverse order, without % and $, and the size is a word (DWORD PTR, 4 bytes) instead of a letter (the l of cmpl). The Assembler: gcc -c​ The assembler translates the assembly into machine code. The result is an object file: machine code that cannot run yet, because it has holes. To call printf, the code needs its address, but printf is not defined in hello.c, so the assembler does not know where it is: it leaves an empty place, and a note with the name printf. The linker fills these holes later. [student@fedora lab07]$ gcc -c hello.c [student@fedora lab07]$ file hello.o hello.o: ELF 64-bit LSB relocatable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), not stripped [student@fedora lab07]$ nm hello.o 0000000000000000 T main U printf nm listed the names (the symbols) of hello.o: T means defined here (in the text, the code), U means used here but undefined. objdump -d hello.o shows the machine code, as bytes, next to the assembly; -M intel uses the Intel syntax. To see each line of C above its machine code, compile with -g and add -S: gcc -g -c hello.c, then objdump -d -S -M intel hello.o. The Linker​ The linker (ld, which gcc runs for you) joins the object files into an executable, and fills in their holes. For every name that an object file uses but does not define (a U in nm), the linker looks for the one place that defines it (a T), in another object file or in a library. If it finds none, it stops with undefined reference; if it finds two, with multiple definition (see Build Errors). printf is defined in the C library, the file libc.so.6, which the linker searches for every program, without being asked. It is a shared library, so the linker does not copy printf into hello: it only writes down that hello needs libc.so.6. [student@fedora lab07]$ gcc hello.o -o hello [student@fedora lab07]$ file hello hello: ELF 64-bit LSB pie executable, x86-64, ..., dynamically linked, ... [student@fedora lab07]$ ldd hello linux-vdso.so.1 (0x00007ffc8d5f2000) libc.so.6 => /lib64/libc.so.6 (0x00007f2b6a200000) /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 (0x00007f2b6a4b1000) gcc saw an object file, not a .c file, so it ran only the linker. ldd listed the libraries that hello needs when it starts: printf is not copied into hello, it stays in libc.so.6, which the system loads every time hello starts. The numbers in parentheses change at every run. With gcc -static, the linker copies printf, and everything that it needs, from the C library into the executable: the program does not need libc.so.6 any more, but it is much larger. On Fedora, -static needs the package glibc-static. The exercises at home and the challenges build their own libraries: the details are in Libraries. tip gcc -save-temps hello.c -o hello runs the four steps and keeps the files of each step: hello.i, hello.s and hello.o.

A real program has many source files. Each part of the program, a module, is a pair of files: File What it has Who uses it Example: lib .h, the header the declarations: what the module offers, without the code; also its #defines and types every .c file that calls the module, with #include lib.h: int sum(int n); .c, the source the definitions: the code of the functions the compiler, which turns it into an object file lib.c: int sum(int n) { ... } Every .c file that uses a module includes its header, so the compiler knows the name and the types of the functions it calls. The examples use the files of ~/lab07/project, a program that adds the numbers from 1 to MAX: project/ ├── main.c # includes lib.h and print.h; main() calls sum() and print_result() ├── lib.h # #define MAX 10, declares sum() ├── lib.c # includes lib.h, defines sum() ├── print.h # declares print_result() └── print.c # includes <stdio.h> and print.h, defines print_result() with printf() ~/lab07/project/lib.h #ifndef LIB_H #define LIB_H #define MAX 10 int sum(int n); #endif #ifndef, #define and #endif are the include guard: if a .c file includes lib.h twice, the second copy is skipped. Every .c file is compiled alone, to its own object file, and the linker joins the object files: [student@fedora project]$ gcc -c main.c [student@fedora project]$ gcc -c lib.c [student@fedora project]$ gcc -c print.c [student@fedora project]$ gcc main.o lib.o print.o -o app [student@fedora project]$ ./app sum = 55 In main.o, sum and print_result are U; the linker found them in lib.o and print.o. This is why every .c file is compiled to its own object file. After a change to print.c, only print.o is out of date, so two commands are enough: gcc -c print.c compiles it again, and gcc main.o lib.o print.o -o app links the program. gcc main.c lib.c print.c -o app gives the same program in one command, but it compiles all the files every time. With three files, this does not matter. The Linux kernel has more than 30 000 .c files: compiling only the ones that changed saves minutes at every build.

These are the messages that the build log of the IDE shows. Who reports the error tells you what is wrong: The message Reported by The cause The fix fatal error: lib.h: No such file or directory preprocessor a wrong name in #include, or the header is in another folder fix the name, or add -I <DIR> error: implicit declaration of function ‘sum’ compiler sum is called, but nothing above the call declares it include the header that declares it error: expected ‘;’ before ‘}’ token compiler a syntax error, on the line it names or on the line before add the missing ; undefined reference to `sum' linker no object file defines sum add the .o file that defines it undefined reference to `sqrt' linker the function is in a library that is not linked add -lm at the end of the command multiple definition of `sum' linker two object files define sum keep only one of them [student@fedora lab07]$ gcc roots.c -o roots /usr/bin/ld: /tmp/ccx5idIu.o: in function `main': roots.c:(.text+0x1c): undefined reference to `sqrt' collect2: error: ld returned 1 exit status [student@fedora lab07]$ gcc roots.c -o roots -lm [student@fedora lab07]$ ./roots sqrt(1) = 1.000 sqrt(2) = 1.414 sqrt(3) = 1.732 sqrt(4) = 2.000 /usr/bin/ld and collect2 mean that the linker failed: compiling worked, but nobody defines sqrt. It is in the math library, libm, which -lm adds. The errors of the preprocessor and of the compiler start with <FILE>:<LINE>:<COLUMN>:, the place of the problem. A warning does not stop the build, but it often shows a bug. Always compile with -Wall, and fix every warning.

In the IDE of the programming course, the code is colored, names are completed and errors are marked while you type. In the terminal, two programs do this together: an editor, and a language server, a program that understands one language. For C, the language server is clangd. The LSP (Language Server Protocol) is the common language between them: any editor that speaks LSP can use any language server. Without it, every editor needs its own plugin for every language. Think of a colleague who reads over your shoulder while you write: the editor is your notebook, and the language server is the colleague, who reads every line and answers your questions about it.
documents.s: An Editor with a Language Server

documents.t: When you open a C file, the editor starts clangd as a child process (lab 03) and talks to it through two pipes (lab 06), in short JSON messages. The editor sends the text after every change and asks questions; clangd answers them, and sends the errors by itself. clangd checks the code while you type, like the compiler, but it does not build anything.

Install clangd (Fedora: sudo dnf install clang-tools-extra; Ubuntu: sudo apt install clangd) and one of these editors: Editor Where it runs What it needs to use clangd vim terminal a plugin, vim-lsp, and about 20 lines in ~/.vimrc nvim 0.11 or newer terminal a few lines in ~/.config/nvim/init.lua hx (Helix) terminal nothing emacs 29 or newer both one line in ~/.emacs.d/init.el code (VS Code) window the extension clangd zed (Zed) window nothing tip nvim, not vim If you like the keys of vim (see Text Editors in lab 06), use nvim: it has the same keys and a language client built in, so its setup is a few lines. vim needs a plugin and about 20 lines of Vimscript. The other editors need almost no setup. Install, configure and check your editor: vim nvim hx emacs VS Code Zed caution This is the hardest setup vim has no language client of its own, and every new feature needs more Vimscript: use nvim instead, with the same editing keys (see the tip above). Install vim (Fedora: sudo dnf install vim-enhanced; Ubuntu: sudo apt install vim) and the plugin vim-lsp, in the folder where vim loads its plugins by itself: git clone https://github.com/prabirshrestha/vim-lsp ~/.vim/pack/lsp/start/vim-lsp Then add these lines to ~/.vimrc: they start clangd for the C files, and give the keys of the table below. ~/.vimrc let g:lsp_diagnostics_virtual_text_enabled = 1 if executable('clangd') au User lsp_setup call lsp#register_server({ \ 'name': 'clangd', \ 'cmd': {server_info->['clangd']}, \ 'allowlist': ['c', 'cpp'], \ }) endif function! s:on_lsp_buffer_enabled() abort setlocal omnifunc=lsp#complete nmap <buffer> gd <plug>(lsp-definition) nmap <buffer> gr <plug>(lsp-references) nmap <buffer> K <plug>(lsp-hover) nmap <buffer> <leader>rn <plug>(lsp-rename) nmap <buffer> <leader>ca <plug>(lsp-code-action) nmap <buffer> ]d <plug>(lsp-next-diagnostic) endfunction augroup lsp_install au! autocmd User lsp_buffer_enabled call s:on_lsp_buffer_enabled() augroup END Check: open a .c file, and run :LspStatus; it shows clangd: running. In the table, \ is the leader key of vim, <leader> in ~/.vimrc. What you want Keys see the errors at the end of the line; ] d goes to the next one see what the name under the cursor is K complete a name in Insert mode, Ctrl+X Ctrl+O go to the definition, come back g d, Ctrl+O list the uses of a name g r rename a name, in every file \ r n apply the fix that it suggests \ c a Install Neovim (Fedora: sudo dnf install neovim). It needs version 0.11 or newer (nvim --version); Ubuntu 24.04 has an older one: use Helix or Zed there. Then add these lines to ~/.config/nvim/init.lua: ~/.config/nvim/init.lua vim.lsp.config('clangd', { cmd = { 'clangd' }, filetypes = { 'c', 'cpp' }, root_markers = { 'compile_commands.json', 'compile_flags.txt', 'Makefile', '.git' }, }) vim.lsp.enable('clangd') vim.diagnostic.config({ virtual_text = true }) Check: open a .c file, and run :checkhealth vim.lsp; it lists clangd among the active clients. Ready-made setups: instead of writing init.lua yourself, you can start from a configuration that already has clangd, completion and a file explorer. They need a recent Neovim and git. Move your ~/.config/nvim and ~/.local/share/nvim aside first, where the setups install their plugins: kickstart.nvim: one file, explained by its comments; the best start if you want to understand your configuration; LazyVim, NvChad and AstroNvim: complete setups, ready to use. Documentation: :help lsp in Neovim (online), and nvim-lspconfig, the settings of many language servers, ready to use. What you want Keys see the errors at the end of the line; ] d goes to the next one see what the name under the cursor is K complete a name in Insert mode, Ctrl+X Ctrl+O go to the definition, come back Ctrl+], Ctrl+T list the uses of a name g r r rename a name, in every file g r n apply the fix that it suggests g r a Install Helix (Fedora: sudo dnf install helix; Ubuntu: sudo snap install --classic helix); its command is hx. It needs no settings: it starts clangd by itself for every .c file. [student@fedora project]$ hx --health c ... Configured language servers: ✓ clangd: /usr/bin/clangd ... Helix found clangd in PATH. A ✘ there means that clangd is not installed. What you want Keys see the errors marked at the left; Space d lists them see what the name under the cursor is Space k complete a name appears while you type go to the definition, come back g d, Ctrl+O list the uses of a name g r rename a name, in every file Space r apply the fix that it suggests Space a Install Emacs (Fedora: sudo dnf install emacs; Ubuntu: sudo apt install emacs). From version 29 it has a language client built in, Eglot, which already knows clangd. This line in ~/.emacs.d/init.el starts it for every C file; if you already have a file ~/.emacs, put the line there instead, because Emacs reads only one of them: ~/.emacs.d/init.el (add-hook 'c-mode-hook 'eglot-ensure) Check: open a .c file (emacs -nw main.c stays in the terminal); the mode line, at the bottom, shows eglot. What you want Keys see the errors underlined; Alt+X flymake-show-buffer-diagnostics lists them see what the name under the cursor is shown at the bottom, by itself complete a name Ctrl+Alt+I go to the definition, come back Alt+., Alt+, list the uses of a name Alt+? rename a name, in every file Alt+X eglot-rename apply the fix that it suggests Alt+X eglot-code-actions Download the .rpm (Fedora) or the .deb (Ubuntu) package from code.visualstudio.com, install it with sudo dnf install ./code-*.rpm (Ubuntu: sudo apt install ./code_*.deb), and add the extension clangd, from the LLVM project, from the Extensions bar: press Ctrl+Shift+X, or click the icon with four squares, on the bar at the left; type clangd in the search box at the top; choose clangd, published by LLVM, and press Install. The same, from the terminal: code --install-extension llvm-vs-code-extensions.vscode-clangd If the extension C/C++ of Microsoft is also installed, the extension clangd asks to turn off its IntelliSense: accept, so that only clangd checks the code. If clangd is not installed, the extension offers to download it: install the package instead, so that every editor uses the same clangd. VSCodium, the same editor without the Microsoft parts, works the same way; its command is codium, not code. Check: open the folder of the project (code ~/lab07/project), then a .c file; the status bar, at the bottom, shows clangd. What you want Keys see the errors red underline; Ctrl+Shift+M lists them see what the name under the cursor i keep the mouse over it, or Ctrl+K Ctrl+I complete a name appears while you type; Ctrl+Space go to the definition, come back F12, Ctrl+Alt+- list the uses of a name Shift+F12 rename a name, in every file F2 apply the fix that it suggests Ctrl+. Install Zed with its script, the same on Fedora and on Ubuntu: curl -f https://zed.dev/install.sh | sh The script installs the command zed in ~/.local/bin; if the shell does not find it, log out and log in again. The script installs the command zed in ~/.local/bin; if the shell does not find it, log out and log in again. Zed works out of the box: it needs no settings and no extension, and starts clangd by itself for every .c file. Check: open the folder of the project (zed ~/lab07/project), then a .c file, and make an error: it is underlined at once. What you want Keys see the errors red underline; Ctrl+Shift+M lists them see what the name under the cursor is keep the mouse over it complete a name appears while you type go to the definition, come back F12, Ctrl+Alt+- list the uses of a name right click, Find All References rename a name, in every file F2 apply the fix that it suggests Ctrl+. When the project has headers in other folders, clangd needs the options of gcc: they are in What clangd Needs to Know, after the Makefile.

After every change you must remember which commands to run again, and in which order. make does it for you. It reads a file named Makefile, from the current directory, that says, for every file to build, what it is made from and which commands make it. Then make runs only the commands that are needed. Think of a recipe book in which each recipe lists its ingredients: to make a cake, you first make the cream it needs, but only if you do not already have fresh cream in the fridge.

A Makefile is a list of rules: target: prerequisites command 1 command 2 Part What it is target the file to build prerequisites the files it is made from, separated by spaces recipe the commands that build it, one per line, each line starting with a TAB The Makefile of hello has two rules: ~/lab07/Makefile hello: hello.o gcc hello.o -o hello hello.o: hello.c gcc -c hello.c hello is linked from hello.o; hello.o is compiled from hello.c. make alone builds the first target, hello; make hello.o builds only hello.o. caution A TAB, not spaces Every line of a recipe starts with a TAB character. With spaces, make stops with Makefile:2: *** missing separator. Stop. Most editors keep the TABs in a file named Makefile; in vim, :set list shows a TAB as ^I.

To build a target, make: builds its prerequisites first, each with its own rule, in the same way; runs the recipe if the target does not exist, or if a prerequisite is newer than the target; otherwise, does nothing: the target is up to date. A prerequisite without a rule, like hello.c, must exist. make compares only the modification times of the files (ls -l --full-time shows them, to the fraction of a second); it never reads the code. [student@fedora lab07]$ make gcc -c hello.c gcc hello.o -o hello [student@fedora lab07]$ make make: 'hello' is up to date. [student@fedora lab07]$ touch hello.c [student@fedora lab07]$ make gcc -c hello.c gcc hello.o -o hello The first make built both files: they did not exist. make prints every command before it runs it. The second make did nothing: hello.c is older than hello.o, and hello.o is older than hello. touch (see touch in lab 02) set the time of hello.c to now, as if you had edited it: hello.c became newer than hello.o, so make compiled it again, and then hello.o was newer than hello. The picture shows the rule that make follows for every target, then the last make, step by step: make keeps a stack of the targets it is working on. It goes down to the prerequisites, then comes back up and runs the recipes that are needed. Command What it does make builds the first target of the Makefile, and only what is out of date make <TARGET> builds <TARGET> make -n shows the commands that it would run, without running them (dry run) make -B builds every target again, even the ones that are up to date make <VAR>=<VALUE> changes a variable for this run only; the Makefile stays the same (see Variables) make -C <DIR> goes to <DIR> first, and works there, as if you ran make in <DIR> make --debug=v explains why it builds, or skips, every target make -j<N> runs up to <N> commands at the same time

For the project, every object file has a rule, and app is linked from the three object files: ~/lab07/project/Makefile app: main.o lib.o print.o gcc main.o lib.o print.o -o app main.o: main.c gcc -c main.c lib.o: lib.c gcc -c lib.c print.o: print.c gcc -c print.c [student@fedora project]$ make gcc -c main.c gcc -c lib.c gcc -c print.c gcc main.o lib.o print.o -o app [student@fedora project]$ touch print.c [student@fedora project]$ make gcc -c print.c gcc main.o lib.o print.o -o app After touch print.c, main.o and lib.o were still up to date: make compiled only print.c, then linked. The three rules of the object files are almost the same. The next three sections make the Makefile shorter.

Inside a recipe, make replaces the automatic variables with the names of the rule: Variable What it means In the rule app: main.o lib.o print.o $@ the target app $< the first prerequisite main.o $^ all the prerequisites main.o lib.o print.o With them, the recipe of app is gcc $^ -o $@, and the recipes of the three object files become the same: gcc -c $< -o $@.

A pattern rule is one rule for many files: % matches any name, the same one in the target and in the prerequisite. %.o: %.c means main.o: main.c, lib.o: lib.c, print.o: print.c, and any other object file. app: main.o lib.o print.o gcc $^ -o $@ %.o: %.c gcc -c $< -o $@ 11 lines became 5. A new module needs only its object file in the list of app. make also has built-in rules: without any rule for main.o, it still compiles main.c, with cc -c. Write your own rules, so that you choose the commands.

A variable keeps a value in one place: write it as NAME = value, and use it as $(NAME). Two names are a convention, and every C programmer expects them: Variable What it holds Usual value CC the C compiler gcc CFLAGS the options of the compiler -Wall -g CC = gcc CFLAGS = -Wall -g app: main.o lib.o print.o $(CC) $^ -o $@ %.o: %.c $(CC) $(CFLAGS) -c $< -o $@ [student@fedora project]$ make -B gcc -Wall -g -c main.c -o main.o gcc -Wall -g -c lib.c -o lib.o gcc -Wall -g -c print.c -o print.o gcc main.o lib.o print.o -o app [student@fedora project]$ make -n -B CFLAGS=-O2 gcc -O2 -c main.c -o main.o ... make printed every command after replacing the variables. CFLAGS=-O2 on the command line replaced the value of the Makefile, without changing the file; -n only showed the commands.

Some targets are not files: they are names for something that you ask make to do. clean deletes what make built: clean: rm -f *.o app make clean runs rm every time, because there is never a file named clean. But if one appears, clean has no prerequisites and the file exists, so it is up to date, and rm does not run: [student@fedora project]$ touch clean [student@fedora project]$ make clean make: 'clean' is up to date. The special target .PHONY lists the targets that are not files: make does not look for a file with their name, and always runs their recipes. The usual phony targets are: Target What it does all builds everything; it is the first target, so make means make all run builds the program, if it is out of date, then runs it clean deletes the files that make built install copies the program into a folder of PATH, so that you can run it by its name from any folder uninstall deletes what install copied ~/lab07/project/Makefile CC = gcc CFLAGS = -Wall -g .PHONY: all run clean all: app run: app ./app app: main.o lib.o print.o $(CC) $^ -o $@ %.o: %.c $(CC) $(CFLAGS) -c $< -o $@ clean: rm -f *.o app [student@fedora project]$ make run ./app sum = 55 [student@fedora project]$ make make: Nothing to be done for 'all'. make run checked app first: it was up to date, so make only ran ./app. all has no recipe, and app was up to date: nothing to do. info These names are a convention, not part of make: every C programmer expects them, but make treats them like any other target. Only the order matters: make alone builds the first target of the Makefile. info These names are a convention, not part of make: every C programmer expects them, but make treats them like any other target.
