A header is also a prerequisite: an object file must be compiled again when a header that its .c file includes changes. With the Makefile above, make does not know that: [student@fedora project]$ sed -i 's/MAX 10/MAX 100/' lib.h [student@fedora project]$ make make: Nothing to be done for 'all'. [student@fedora project]$ ./app sum = 55 The sum of the numbers from 1 to 100 is 5050, but main.o was not compiled again: lib.h is not in any rule. The dependencies follow the #include lines. Look at the #include lines of every .c file, and add each header to the rule of its object file: main.o: lib.h print.h lib.o: lib.h print.o: print.h These rules have no recipe: they only add prerequisites, and the recipe still comes from %.o: %.c. Put them at the end of the Makefile, so that all stays the first target. [student@fedora project]$ make gcc -Wall -g -c main.c -o main.o gcc -Wall -g -c lib.c -o lib.o gcc main.o lib.o print.o -o app [student@fedora project]$ ./app sum = 5050 main.c and lib.c include lib.h: their object files were compiled again; print.o was kept. caution A header goes on the rule of an object file, never on the rule of the executable: with app: main.o lib.o print.o lib.h, make only links again the old main.o, which still has MAX equal to 10.

clangd checks each file as gcc would compile it, so it needs the same options, like -I <DIR>. Without them, a header from another folder gives '<HEADER>' file not found in the editor, even if make works. Give it the options in a file in the folder of the project: File What it has How you make it Use it when compile_flags.txt the options of gcc, one per line, the same for every file by hand, in the editor: for example, the line -Iinclude all the files use the same options compile_commands.json the exact gcc command of every file, as make ran it make clean, then bear -- make; again after you add a file the files use different options, or a rename must change every file bear (Fedora: sudo dnf install bear; Ubuntu: sudo apt install bear) writes down every command that make runs, so start from a clean build. With compile_commands.json, clangd also knows the files that you did not open: a rename changes all of them. It keeps what it learns, the index of the project, in the folder .cache, which does not go in the repository (see Saving Versions). clangd --check=<FILE> checks a file in the terminal; its last line ends with All checks completed, 0 errors when the file has no error.

A debugger runs another program under its control: it stops it at a line, runs it one line at a time, and shows its variables, while it runs. It is faster than adding printf lines and compiling again. gdb is the debugger of GNU. It needs the program built with -g, which adds the debug information: which machine code comes from which line, and where every variable is. The Makefile of the project already has -g in CFLAGS. Command Short What it does gdb ./app starts gdb with the program; the program does not run yet break <FUNCTION>, break <FILE>:<LINE> b sets a breakpoint: the program will stop there, before that line runs break <PLACE> if <CONDITION> stops there only when the C condition is true: break sum if n > 5 watch <VARIABLE> stops every time the variable changes, and prints its old and its new value delete <N> d deletes breakpoint number <N>; without <N>, deletes them all run r starts the program; it runs until a breakpoint, or until it ends next n runs the line that gdb showed; a function that it calls runs whole, without stopping step s runs the line that gdb showed, but stops inside the function that it calls finish fin runs until the current function returns, and prints the value it returns continue c runs until the next breakpoint, or until the program ends print <EXPRESSION> p prints a variable, or any C expression: print n * 2 backtrace bt prints the call stack: the current function, the one that called it, and so on up, down moves to the function that called this one, or back, to print its variables quit q quits gdb, and stops the program if it still runs [student@fedora project]$ gdb -q ./app Reading symbols from ./app... (gdb) break sum Breakpoint 1 at 0x1171: file lib.c, line 5. (gdb) run Starting program: /home/student/lab07/project/app ... Breakpoint 1, sum (n=10) at lib.c:5 5 int s = 0; (gdb) print n $1 = 10 (gdb) backtrace #0 sum (n=10) at lib.c:5 #1 0x0000555555555150 in main () at main.c:6 (gdb) continue Continuing. sum = 55 [Inferior 1 (process 4211) exited normally] (gdb) quit -q (quiet) skipped the text about the license. break sum set a breakpoint on the first line of the body of sum, line 5 of lib.c; the addresses and the number of the process change from one computer to another. The program stopped before line 5 ran; backtrace showed that main, at line 6 of main.c, called sum. continue let the program run to its end. note On Fedora and Ubuntu, gdb may ask Enable debuginfod for this session? (y or [n]): answer n. It offers to download the debug information of the system libraries, which this lab does not need; skip the lines about Missing ... debuginfo in the same way. gdb -tui shows the source code above the commands.

Git is a version control system: it keeps the history of the files of a project. You can go back to any version, see what changed and why, and work on the same code together with other people. The folder with the files and their history (in the hidden folder .git) is a repository. A commit is a snapshot of all the files, with an author, a date and a message; its name is a hash, like ed6ba3b. Think of the save points of a game: you save when things work, and you can always come back to a save point. A change goes through three places on your computer: you edit the files, git add puts them in the staging area (what the next commit will have), and git commit saves the commit in the repository. Command What it does git config --global user.name "<NAME>" your name, written in every commit; once per computer git config --global user.email "<EMAIL>" your email, written in every commit; once per computer git init turns the current folder into a repository git status shows the changed files, and what is in the staging area git add <FILE> adds the changes of <FILE> to the staging area; git add . adds all git commit -m "<MESSAGE>" saves the staging area as a commit git diff shows the changes that are not in the staging area yet git log --oneline shows the commits, one per line, the newest first git restore <FILE> throws away the changes of <FILE> that are not in the staging area; you cannot get them back git switch -c <BRANCH>, git switch <BRANCH> creates a branch and goes to it; goes to a branch git merge <BRANCH> brings the commits of <BRANCH> into the current branch The files that make builds can always be built again: they do not go in the repository, and neither does the folder .cache, where clangd keeps its index. The file .gitignore lists, one per line, the names (or the globs) that git ignores: [student@fedora project]$ git init Initialized empty Git repository in /home/student/lab07/project/.git/ [student@fedora project]$ printf '*.o
app
.cache/
' > .gitignore [student@fedora project]$ git add . [student@fedora project]$ git status --short A .gitignore A Makefile A lib.c A lib.h A main.c A print.c A print.h [student@fedora project]$ git commit -m "Add the sum program" [main (root-commit) ed6ba3b] Add the sum program 7 files changed, 60 insertions(+) ... git status --short showed A (added) for the files in the staging area; the object files and app are not there, because of .gitignore. The hash of your commit is different: it depends on the content, the author and the time.

The First Steps use only your computer; the exercises at home and the challenges also use GitHub. A commit stays on your computer. A remote is a copy of the repository on a server, such as GitHub, GitLab or Codeberg: you push your commits to it, and pull from it the commits of your colleagues. A colleague starts by cloning the repository: a copy of the files and of the whole history, connected to the same remote, origin. Think of a shared folder in the cloud that keeps every save point, with its author. Command What it does git remote add origin <URL> connects the repository to the remote <URL>, under the name origin git remote -v lists the remotes git push -u origin main sends main to origin the first time; -u remembers it, then git push is enough git push origin <BRANCH> sends another branch git pull brings the new commits of origin, and merges them into the current branch git clone <URL> <DIR> copies the repository into <DIR>, with origin already set git branch -d <BRANCH> deletes a local branch that is merged git push origin --delete <BRANCH> deletes a branch on the remote git config --global pull.rebase false git pull merges when both sides have new commits; once per computer GitHub does not accept your password in the terminal. Use an SSH key: a pair of files, a private key that never leaves your computer, and a public key that you give to GitHub. With a key, the URL of a repository is git@github.com:<USER>/<REPO>.git. Create the key once per computer: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "<EMAIL>" # press Enter at every question cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub # paste it in GitHub: Settings, SSH and GPG keys, New SSH key ssh -T git@github.com # answer yes the first time When GitHub knows your key, ssh -T git@github.com prints Hi <USER>! You've successfully authenticated, but GitHub does not provide shell access. A pull request (PR) is a request, made on GitHub, to merge a branch into main. Your colleagues read the changes in the tab Files changed, comment on them, and press Merge pull request; then everybody runs git pull. The rule of most teams: do not commit on main directly; create a branch, push it, and open a pull request. When two people change the same lines, git pull cannot choose between them, and stops with a conflict: [student@fedora bob]$ git pull ... CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in motto.txt Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result. [student@fedora bob]$ cat motto.txt <<<<<<< HEAD keep it clear ======= keep it short >>>>>>> 6c37dc458b34401722a29eace880dec81e97dffb Between <<<<<<< and ======= is your version, between ======= and >>>>>>> the version that came from origin. Edit the file until it has the right text and no marker line, then git add it and run git commit: the result is a merge commit, with two parents.

note Going deeper You do not need this section for the exercises of the lab, the 🧪 First Steps. Read it at home: the 🏠 Going Further exercises and the 📝 Challenges use it. A library is a file with compiled functions, ready to be used by other programs: printf is in the C library, sqrt in the math library. There are two kinds: Static library Shared library the file lib<NAME>.a, an archive of object files lib<NAME>.so, a shared object, ready to be loaded the linker copies the functions into the executable only writes down that the executable needs the library when the program starts nothing more to load: the code is already in the executable the loader (ld-linux-x86-64.so.2) finds the library, and loads it a new version of the library link every program again every program uses it at its next start the size large executables: every program has its own copy small executables: one copy, on the disk and in memory, for all programs if the library is missing the program still runs the program does not start: error while loading shared libraries By default, gcc links the C library as a shared library. -static copies it in: [student@fedora lab07]$ gcc hello.c -o hello-dynamic [student@fedora lab07]$ gcc -static hello.c -o hello-static [student@fedora lab07]$ stat -c '%s %n' hello-dynamic hello-static 8880 hello-dynamic 650832 hello-static [student@fedora lab07]$ ldd hello-static not a dynamic executable The two programs come from the same source, with the same command; only -static differs. hello-static is about 70 times larger: it carries its own copy of printf, and of everything that printf needs. The sizes change from one system to another, and from one processor to another. hello-static is still smaller than the C library (stat -L -c '%s' /lib64/libc.so.6 prints more than 1 MiB): the linker copied only the parts of the library that the program uses. You can build your own libraries. -l<NAME> links lib<NAME>.so or, if there is none, lib<NAME>.a; it looks for them in the folders given with -L <DIR>, then in the folders of the system (/usr/lib64 on Fedora): Command What it does ar rcs libsum.a lib.o creates the static library libsum.a from lib.o ar t libsum.a lists the object files of the archive gcc -fPIC -c lib.c compiles code that works at any address (Position Independent Code), as a shared library needs gcc -shared lib.o -o libsum.so creates the shared library libsum.so gcc main.o print.o -L. -lsum -o app links app with libsum from the current folder (.) LD_LIBRARY_PATH=. ./app runs app, and lets the loader also look for libraries in . [student@fedora project]$ gcc -fPIC -c lib.c [student@fedora project]$ gcc -shared lib.o -o libsum.so [student@fedora project]$ gcc main.o print.o -L. -lsum -o app [student@fedora project]$ ./app ./app: error while loading shared libraries: libsum.so: cannot open shared object file: No such file or directory [student@fedora project]$ LD_LIBRARY_PATH=. ./app sum = 55 -L. told the linker where libsum.so is, but not the loader: when app starts, the loader looks only in the folders of the system. LD_LIBRARY_PATH (see man ld.so) adds folders for one command; installing the library in /usr/lib64 is the other way.

Do these exercises in order, during the lab. Each one starts with what it wants you to achieve, and tries one idea from the lab: read the section linked under its goal if you get stuck. Run the commands in ~/lab07, unless the exercise says otherwise. The practice tree: Check that the tools are installed, and create the files that the other exercises use, in ~/lab07. → Fedora and Ubuntu print the version of gcc, make, gdb, git and clangd; install the ones that are missing; run these commands (copy them from the browser with Ctrl+C and paste them in the terminal with Ctrl+Shift+V): mkdir -p ~/lab07/project cd ~/lab07 cat > hello.c << 'END' #include <stdio.h> #define TIMES 3 int main(void) { // say hello a few times for (int i = 0; i < TIMES; i++) { printf("Hello, %d!
", i); } return 0; } END printf '#!/bin/bash
echo "Hello from bash!"
' > hello.sh chmod +x hello.sh cat > roots.c << 'END' #include <stdio.h> #include <math.h> int main(void) { for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++) { printf("sqrt(%d) = %.3f
", i, sqrt(i)); } return 0; } END cd project cat > main.c << 'END' #include "lib.h" #include "print.h" int main(void) { int total = sum(MAX); print_result("sum", total); return 0; } END printf '%s
' '#ifndef LIB_H' '#define LIB_H' '#define MAX 10' 'int sum(int n);' '#endif' > lib.h cat > lib.c << 'END' #include "lib.h" int sum(int n) { int s = 0; for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) { s = s + i; } return s; } END printf '%s
' '#ifndef PRINT_H' '#define PRINT_H' \ 'void print_result(const char *label, int value);' '#endif' > print.h cat > print.c << 'END' #include <stdio.h> #include "print.h" void print_result(const char *label, int value) { printf("%s = %d
", label, value); } END cd ~/lab07 list the files of ~/lab07 and of ~/lab07/project. Hint Most commands print their version with --version. The packages are in Fedora and Ubuntu. Check gcc, make, gdb, git and clangd each print a version with --version. The commands print nothing. ~/lab07 has hello.c, hello.sh, roots.c and the folder project; project has lib.c, lib.h, main.c, print.c and print.h. Compiling Without the IDE: Build hello.c and run it in the terminal, compare it with a script, and find out why the program starts with ./. → Compiled and Interpreted Languages · Compiling a C Program run hello.sh; compile hello.c into the executable hello, and run it; with one command, print the type of hello.sh, of hello and of /usr/bin/bash, the program that runs the script; compile hello.c again without choosing the name of the output; run the file that gcc made, then delete it; run hello only by its name, without ./; then go to your home directory, and run hello from there, without going back to ~/lab07. Hint man file; Compiling a C Program: the option -o; The PATH Search in lab 04. Check ./hello.sh prints Hello from bash!; ./hello prints Hello, 0!, Hello, 1! and Hello, 2!. hello.sh is a Bourne-Again shell script, ASCII text executable; hello and /usr/bin/bash are each an ELF 64-bit LSB pie executable, .... Without -o, the executable is a.out. bash: hello: command not found (Fedora may offer to install the package hello: answer N); from ~, lab07/hello prints the same 3 lines. Why: hello and bash are machine code, run by the processor; the script is text, read by bash. The shell looks for a command name only in the folders of PATH, and ~/lab07 is not one of them; a path with a / runs directly. Inside the pipeline: Look at the files that the first three steps of the pipeline write for hello.c. → The Preprocessor · The Compiler · The Assembler stop gcc after the preprocessor, and write the result to hello.i; count the lines of hello.c and of hello.i, and find the declaration of printf in hello.i; look at the last lines of hello.i: find what TIMES and the comment became; stop gcc after the compiler, with the lines of C written as comments in hello.s; find the line that calls printf, the line that compares i with 2, and the line of C that each one comes from; write hello.s again, in the Intel syntax, and find the same two lines; stop gcc after the assembler; print the type of hello.o, and list its symbols: find the one that is defined in it, and the one that it only uses. Hint The tables of The Compilation Pipeline and The Compiler; grep, tail and wc from lab 06; man nm: search for "U". Check hello.c has 12 lines; hello.i has several hundred (the number depends on the C library); the declaration is extern int printf (const char *__restrict __format, ...);. The loop has i < 3, and the comment is gone. gcc -S -fverbose-asm hello.c: call printf@PLT is under # hello.c:9:, the printf, and cmpl $2, -4(%rbp) under # hello.c:8:, the for (on ARM: bl printf and cmp w0, 2, after //). gcc -S -masm=intel hello.c: call printf@PLT and cmp DWORD PTR -4[rbp], 2 (on ARM, gcc says unrecognized command-line option: ARM has only one syntax). hello.o: ELF 64-bit LSB relocatable, ...; T main is defined in hello.o, U printf is only used. Why: the preprocessor only changes the text; the compiler and the assembler translate it, but leave a hole for printf, which the linker fills. The linker: Turn the object file into a program, find out which library it needs, and compare it with a static build of the same program. → The Linker link hello.o into hello, run it, and print its type; list the libraries that hello loads when it starts; compile hello.c into hello with one command that also keeps the files of every step; list them, then delete hello.i, hello.s and hello.o; build hello-static from hello.c, with the C library copied in, and run it; compare its size with the size of hello, in bytes, and list its libraries. Hint The Linker; man ldd; man gcc: search for -static (on Fedora, install glibc-static first); stat -c '%s %n' prints the size of a file, in bytes (lab 05). Check hello prints the 3 lines; file says ELF 64-bit LSB pie executable, dynamically linked. libc.so.6 => /lib64/libc.so.6 (Ubuntu: /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6): the library with printf. gcc -save-temps hello.c -o hello keeps hello.i, hello.s and hello.o. gcc -static hello.c -o hello-static; it prints the same 3 lines. hello has less than 20 KiB, hello-static several hundred KiB, tens of times more (the numbers depend on the system); ldd hello-static prints not a dynamic executable. Why: hello-static carries its own copy of printf; hello loads it from libc.so.6 every time it starts. Several source files: In ~/lab07/project, build app from three source files, then rebuild it after a change, with as few commands as possible. → Several Source Files compile each .c file into its object file, then link the three object files into app; run it; with your editor, change print.c so that the program prints sum: 55 instead of sum = 55; rebuild app with only the commands that are needed, and run it; change print.c back, and rebuild app in the same way. Hint Several Source Files: which object file depends on print.c? Check app prints sum = 55. print.c has the line printf("%s: %d
", label, value);. Two commands are enough: gcc -c print.c, then gcc main.o lib.o print.o -o app; app prints sum: 55. The same two commands; app prints sum = 55 again. Why: only print.o is made from print.c; the other object files are still up to date. Build errors: Cause three errors, one at a time, and find out which step of the pipeline reports each of them. → Build Errors compile roots.c into roots; read the error, fix the command, and run roots; in project, link app from main.o and print.o only; in project, rename lib.h to lib.h.bak and compile main.c; then rename it back; for each error, write down the step that reported it. Hint The table of Build Errors; ld and collect2 are the linker. The cc1 line of step 2 starts with its full path, and gcc -print-prog-name=cc1 prints it too: on Fedora, /usr/libexec/gcc/x86_64-redhat-linux/<VERSION>/cc1; on Ubuntu, a similar folder with x86_64-linux-gnu. Why: gcc is a driver: it runs the preprocessor and the compiler (both in cc1), the assembler (as) and the linker (collect2, then ld). ", SQUARE(1 + 2)); return 0; } END compile it and run it; look at the line of printf after the preprocessor; fix the macro, so that the program prints 9. ", 1 + 2 * 1 + 2); With #define SQUARE(x) ((x) * (x)), it prints 9. Why: the preprocessor only replaces text; then C computes * before +, so the macro needs the parentheses. Use the last 5 minutes of the lab to answer these questions together with your colleagues and the teaching assistant. There are no wrong answers for the last two. What is the difference between a compiled and an interpreted program? Which one is hello, and which one is hello.sh? What are the four steps of gcc, and which file comes out of each of them? Why is printf a U symbol in hello.o? Who finds it, and where? What goes in a .h file, and what in a .c file? Why do you compile every .c file to its own object file? How do you know, from a build error, which step reported it? What does a language server do, and how does the editor talk to it? How does make decide if it runs a recipe? Why does clean need .PHONY, and on which rule does a header go? What is the difference between git add and git commit? Why are the object files not in the repository? Which build error surprised you most today? Which tool of this lab will you use for your next C homework?
